Bruno Guimaraes’ return to St James’ Park in Arsenal colours was meant to rub salt into the wounds of Newcastle’s summer exodus, but it galvanised the Magpies who channeled the emotion into a second-half comeback.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It was, for many, the moment Newcastle United ceased to be a force in English football. Bruno Guimaraes’ move to Arsenal was traumatic, and from the club are yet to fully recover.

He was the best player, the talisman, the captain and the one big hope. Without him, an entirely new identity needs to be forged. But Newcastle, and new manager Matthias Jaissle have floundered ever since they parted ways.

Arsenal’s trip north was always going to be about one man. Guimaraes hasn’t been universally derided by Newcastle fans in the way Alexander Isak was, and was made clear by a low key, if still frosty reception when he stepped off the team bus. It was more pantomime than persona non grata.

His exit arguably cut deeper than Isak’s, and those of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali earlier in the summer, but has polarised the fanbase.

For some, his service in leading Newcastle to their first domestic trophy cements his legacy regardless of how ill-timed and controversial his departure was. With so much change at the club going on around him, compounded by the resignation of Eddie Howe in late July, it became clear Guimaraes’ ambitions would no longer be realised on Tyneside.

Seeing Isak, Tonali and Gordon leave with a chance of winning trophies, doubling their wages or both will have stung for the Brazilian. When he arrived in January 2022, he genuinely believed Newcastle would be able to win the Champions League.

Suddenly, they were proudly and publicly embracing a trading model in the transfer market, ripping up their previous approach and starting again. Guimaraes was still central to their plans, but at 28 years of age (now 29), he could no longer wait for phase two of the Newcastle project, especially when promises from phase one remained unfulfilled.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But over the last four years, he went above and beyond other imports when it came to building a relationship with supporters, talking openly about being an adopted Geordie and wanting to emulate Alan Shearer in becoming a lasting hero.

It was that strength of feeling which Newcastle hoped would coax him into staying another season and led to supporters truly believing in loyalty. But in their time of need, the captain abandoned ship. He was well within his rights to depart, and it is hard to criticise given Arsenal already look like Premier League champions elect.

Yet, having talked up his love for life at Newcastle in the build up, reaffirming how difficult it was to leave, he couldn’t have complained when he was cast in the role of villain.

If his afternoon was summed up in one moment, though, it was his former midfield protege at Newcastle, tapping him on the back as Harvey Barnes swept home a second half equaliser.

Malick Thiaw went on to put the home side in front, only for Noni Madueke to restore parity once again. It was a slow burn, but ultimately, Guimaraes’ presence united Newcastle on the pitch and in the stands.

The expectation was it would be instant and Arsenal would be under siege from a black and white storm whipped up by anger in his direction. Instead, in the first half, it was tame, and when Eberechi Eze opened the scoring, it felt like game over already.

There have been reports in recent weeks suggesting the players do not understand Jaissle’s methods. It certainly felt like that at times; Lukas Hornicek, required to confidently play out from the back, looked shaken every time he had the ball at his feet.

Joe Willock was seen asking questions on his role more than once; Jaissle looked on full of exasperation but, it seemed, with very few answers. A third meek home defeat in succession seemed a formality. Once the game restarted, though, everything shifted.

Jaissle, to his credit, made bold choices, bringing off the one bright spark in the first half, Sean Steur and replacing him with Jacob Ramsey. Tino Livramento and Anthony Elanga were also introduced and Newcastle came alive.

The power, the drive and the ferocity of St James’ Park spurred them on. Suddenly, Jaissle’s approach seemed clear; there was something tangible to build from, a blueprint.

“Everything started with the press,” Thiaw said after the game. “If you win the ball high and early, there is space to attack vertically and directly. It is about how you work off the ball.

“The manager kept it really calm at half time, he knew what we had to do and made good changes. When you are a squad, everybody has to be ready. We used [the crowd’s reaction to Guimaraes] as fuel and we felt that on the pitch.”

Thiaw is one of the players who has stepped into what Jaissle called a “leadership vacuum” in the squad after Guimaraes left. He insists the squad is still backing their manager.

“There are always noises in football, especially outside of the locker room,” he added. “We know what we have to do and what we have to deliver. We are giving everything for the club and the manager.

“If we don’t believe, who will? We will keep improving and we need them. We are all in this together.”

Starting with Arsenal, there is a run of four very tough and potentially season-defining games for Jaissle and Newcastle. Brighton follows, before two home games in a week against Manchester United and Sunderland. It is still far from perfect, but green shoots of optimism may just be emerging.

#898. Bruno Fernandes has huge question to ponder on emotional return to Sporting

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Man United captain has been one of the most visible faces of the club’s decline, yet consistently their best player – now he must decide what comes next

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

In the modern Manchester United, it sometimes seems that the bad news comes ever sooner after the good. There is less time to enjoy it before the unwanted reality check. So it was that, when much of Sky Sports descended on Carrington on Friday and chief executive Omar Berrada revealed they were in talks with Bruno Fernandes about a new deal, the question was put to the captain.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said. And if it was a partial answer, saying that the club were keen to extend their relationship but not revealing if he was, nor was there much encouragement to be derived from his explanation. “I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.”

A couple of days later came a result to underline the wisdom of waiting. Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing at Liverpool increased the chances United will be in the Championship, rather than the Champions League, next season. At the least, Fernandes should put his future on hold before working out which division they will be in.

His next transfer may come next summer, when his contract expires – though United have the option to extend it by a further year – but his last move remains his January 2020 switch from Sporting CP. Wednesday night gives him a first chance return to his former club. It could be a triumphant comeback: Fernandes remains among Sporting’s greatest exports and he is still the only unqualified success in United’s recruitment since Sir Alex Ferguson retired.

It was at Sporting that he started scoring at a rate that is almost unrivalled among midfielders: 33 goals in the 2018-19 season, a further 15 in a few months before United made their move.

Almost seven years on, Fernandes goes back on the brink of milestones: one away from a century of Portugal caps, a hat-trick short of 200 club career goals, the last 113 of them for United.

But individual achievements seem to outnumber the collective feats. That is no criticism: at times it has felt as though Fernandes has prevented things from getting worse for United. He has won the FA Cup and the Carabao Cup but, in other eras, that would not be much to show for seven seasons at Old Trafford.

He won the PFA Player of the Year and Footballer of the Year awards last season; they had the air of lifetime achievement awards, as much as recognition for his record-breaking tally of 21 Premier League assists. He has won United’s player-of-the-year award a record five times: but previously, there was more competition. Paul Scholes, for example, never won it.

The contrarian notion United would be better off without him looks increasingly fanciful when the shortcomings of others are ever more apparent. Fernandes has a petulant streak and a capacity to give the ball away in his attempts to make something happen; yet when he criticised Michael Carrick’s tactics after the defeat to Como and the manager responding by benching his skipper, United were hopeless against Bournemouth.

Mauricio Pochettino marked his arrival at Old Trafford by confirming Fernandes as hius captain. He has now worn the armband under eight managers or caretakers – Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Ralf Rangnick, Erik ten Hag, Ruud van Nistelrooy, Ruben Amorim, Darren Fletcher, Carrick and Pochettino – whereas arguably United’s greatest captain, Roy Keane, only did so under one.

It is another indication of instability and underachievement. As Fernandes implied on Friday, he has made sacrifices to stay at United. He could have had a warmer climate elsewhere, he said. He could have made more money, too: the Saudi Pro-League, in particular, would have been more lucrative. Galatasaray might have been.

The sense, perhaps, is that Fernandes, more than United, has to decide what comes next. In footballing lexicon, players earn new contracts. Maybe, though, the club have to earn the right for a deal that is proffered to be signed.

Fernandes will turn 33 next September. His next contract will probably be the last at anything near his peak, even for a man who, since the start of the 2017-18 season, has averaged over 60 games a year for club and country.

And yet, he may note, he might have played more in the Champions League simply by staying at Sporting. They were quarter-finalists last season, when United were not in the competition. They are three points ahead of United now. They stand a far better chance of being in the Champions League next season.

Fernandes has been one of the most visible faces in the decline of United, but also the man who did more than anyone else to fight it. It has given him a form of greatness but perhaps, as he returns to Portugal, it could make him ponder the career choices he has made, and will make.

Ali Dia has gone down in folklore for his absolutely bizarre appearance for Southampton in 1996

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We probably don't need to recap the story, do we? But just in case...

It was 30 years ago exactly, back on 23 November, 1996, when Ali Dia made perhaps the most notorious appearance in the history of Premier League football.

Dia had purported to be the cousin of George Weah to get himself a trial at Graeme Souness' Southampton, and incredibly ended up coming on in place of the injured Matt Le Tissier, only to later be subbed back off hauled back off in the 85th minute of a 2-0 defeat to Leeds.

Dia looked like he'd struggle to play in a Sunday league team, never mind a top-flight outfit - but as Souness explained to FourFourTwo: "That was portrayed like we'd been conned, but no-one was conned.

"Someone phoned up pretending to be George Weah, but we were getting players in every month to come on trial, because we had no money – that's where we got Eyal Berkovic." (Wonder who Berkovic's agent pretended to be?)

"When we got the call about Dia, I said, 'Get him in'.

"Within the first five minutes of a small-sided game at training, I realised he wasn't good enough for us.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"But we didn't have enough players for training sessions, so we said, 'We'll keep him until the end of the week, then we'll tell him'.

"That week we got more and more injuries, to the point where my coach Terry Cooper said, 'We're going to have to have that clown on the bench'.

"I said, 'We can't'. He said, 'We haven't got any players'.

"He was on the bench against Leeds, then Matt Le Tissier comes off injured and I've got a choice between a centre-half, a full-back or a defensive midfielder [or Dia].

"I said, 'Stick Dia on, he'll run about, hopefully occupy their back four'.

"He did that, but he was out of his depth."

#896. William D. Nordhaus obituary: economist whose tools transformed climate policy

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Eli P. Fenichel is a professor of natural-resource economics at Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut.

Lint Barrage is associate professor and chair of energy and climate economics at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, Zurich, Switzerland.

Robert J. Gordon is emeritus professor in the social sciences at Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois.

Credit: Monica Jorge/New York Times/Redux/eyevine

William (Bill) Nordhaus was an economist known for introducing climate change into economic analysis, earning him the 2018 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Profoundly curious and able to distill complex issues to their core, Nordhaus produced groundbreaking scholarship powered by his joy of discovery, dedication to getting things right and commitment to ensuring that science serves society.

His research shaped our understanding of what drives economic growth and innovation. He realized that omitting the environment from economic measurement would send the wrong signals about the directions of economic growth and, therefore, pioneered more-inclusive ways to measure growth.

To build a better world, stop chasing economic growth

To build a better world, stop chasing economic growth

Nordhaus was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico. His father developed a ski area to the east of the city, and as a child, Nordhaus tried to derive models of snowfall. He earned an undergraduate degree in economics from Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1963, before moving to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, where he completed his PhD in 1967 under the supervision of future Nobel prizewinner Robert Solow. He then returned to Yale as an assistant professor and spent the rest of his academic career there.

Nordhaus quickly made a name for himself by developing an early rigorous model for endogenous growth — that which occurs inside an economic system, rather than being driven by external factors. Before then, economic models had assumed that the rate of change in technology was independent of the economy.

Nordhaus’s PhD work showed that the pace of innovation depended on economic incentives, which could be altered by policy, such as through the patent system. His model also projected that research would face diminishing returns, with new ideas getting harder to find — an idea that was validated 40 years later.

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality

Why we need an International Panel on Inequality

Next, he questioned the nature of economic growth. He recalled being inspired by an article in an in-flight magazine that described gross national product (GNP) as gross national pollution. In a 1972 article titled ‘Is Growth Obsolete?’, Nordhaus and economist James Tobin wrote that GNP exaggerates economic benefits by omitting environmental damage by “treating as free things which are not really free” and that “this practice gives the wrong signals for the directions of economic growth”. GNP also understates some of the benefits of economic growth, such as increased household well-being, from inventions such as electricity and home appliances.

This work alone gave rise to three influential lines of research: climate economics, the role of national accounts in measuring sustainable development and the importance of including new goods in measures of national income and economic well-being.

Nordhaus also considered the role of innovation. In a 1996 article on the history of the price of lighting, he measured the output and cost of various sources of light across human history (see go.nature.com/478rjyh). He showed that the light output per unit of energy of the compact fluorescent bulb was about 30,000 times greater than that of our distant ancestors’ fire.

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations

#895. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

Forget the Premier League procession, Serie A is European football’s greatest spectacle this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're looking for jeopardy at the top of the Premier League this season, you're looking in the wrong place.

Arsenal, already reigning champions, have so far turned their title defence into an autumn stroll, swatting aside challengers with efficiency, threatening to wrap up another crown at a canter before winter is even through.

For genuine drama and unpredictability in 2026/27, the centre of gravity in European football has shifted south. Serie A, once a league renowned for miserly defences and low-scoring contests, is serving up the most compelling, wide-open title race on the continent.

If any proof was needed that Italian football has buried its old catenaccio stereotype for good, Sunday evening's 4-4 draw between Atalanta and Inter Milan delivered it.

Far from being a cagey affair, it was pure mayhem with two heavyweights trading blows right up until the final whistle.

That eight-goal epic was no anomaly, either because across Europe’s top five leagues this campaign, Serie A actually leads the way for entertainment in front of goal, averaging 3.08 goals per match.

The Italian top flight is comfortably ahead of the Bundesliga (2.94), the Premier League (2.81), Ligue 1 (2.72) and La Liga (2.56). So, forget 1-0 defensive masterclasses, modern calcio is all about goals.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Better still, the table looks like a throwback to the division’s 1990s golden era. Only a handful of points separates the leading pack, with several of Italy’s biggest and best-supported institutions - from Milan and Naples to Turin and the capital - are engaged in a multi-club scrap for the Scudetto.

A key reason for that is the capital roaring back to life. Both Roma and Lazio remain unbeaten 12 games into the season, having spent too many recent campaigns watching their northern rivals monopolise domestic success. The Eternal City’s old powers are title contenders once again, playing with renewed swagger.

The beauty of this Serie A season lies just as much in its new blood as its established giants, becaause perched on the periphery of the title race are Como, one of European football’s coolest and most compelling stories.

Their lakeside glamour is neatly juxtaposed by a smart, progressive sporting project and exciting football. They are doing their best to crash the elite party without a hint of an inferiority complex.

For nearly a decade, Juventus’ run of nine consecutive titles drained the suspense from Italian football. Serie A has since become one of Europe’s most competitive major leagues, albeit without continental success. Over the past five years, three different clubs - Inter, AC Milan and Napoli - have lifted the trophy, and not once has it returned to Turin, nor does it look as though that'll be the case this season, either.

Of course, the Premier League still boasts the deepest pockets and the best marketing machine, but when the title race is effectively over before December, spectacle suffers. In Italy, the potential for plot twists retains the intrigue and drama.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#893. Millwall punished with partial stadium closure over ‘ableist and homophobic chanting’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Millwall will have to close part of their stadium when they host Sheffield United next month

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Millwall have been ordered to partially close their stadium after being found guilty of discriminatory chanting by supporters.

A regulatory commission proved two charges relating to disability and sexual orientation discrimination during January’s fixture against Charlton. Consequently, the Sky Bet Championship team will host Sheffield United with a reduced capacity at The Den on 8 December.

Four blocks inside the Dockers Stand will be shut for the visit of the Blades.

The club have also been fined £70,000, issued an extended FA Action Plan, and handed another partial stadium closure, suspended until the end of next season.

A club statement read: "Both chants are discriminatory and offensive, and the club condemns them in the strongest possible terms.

"Ableist and homophobic chanting, as well as any other form of discriminatory chanting, has no place in football or society.

"Any individual identified as engaging in such abuse will face the consequences.

"The club will continue the significant work already achieved under its dedicated anti-discrimination campaign, ‘All ’Wall’, while continuously reviewing and enhancing best practice to ensure The Den is always a welcoming environment."

Anti-discrimination group Kick It Out said it “welcomes greater accountability for discriminatory mass chanting and supports greater collaboration between clubs and governing bodies to tackle this serious issue”.

It added: “Last season, we received a record number of mass chanting reports across football, including racist, sexist and misogynistic, homophobic, ableist and faith-based abuse. This is why we’re conducting further research and campaigning to show its impact on communities and ensure more consistent action from clubs and authorities.

“Education has a key role here, both for fans, so that they know the impact and consequences of discriminatory chanting, and clubs, so they can proactively help to reduce its prevalence. We stand ready to support football in helping eradicate this problem.”

Last month, Millwall’s match against Swansea was halted for seven minutes after an allegation of racist abuse from the crowd towards Swans substitute Eom Ji Sung was reported by the Welsh club to officials.

Referee Edward Duckworth halted the match in the 65th minute and walked to the dug-outs to speak with Lions boss Alex Neil, Swans counterpart Vitor Matos and fourth official Ruebyn Ricardo.

When play eventually resumed it was announced in the stadium that there had been a report of racist chanting, adding that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.

#892. Any regrets, Mauricio? Man Utd are deep in relegation battle after Anfield farce

The Liverpool fans did not miss a beat. They never do. “Poch is at the wheel,” they goaded as this calamity unfolded. But at the wheel of what, a clown car? The look of thunder on Mauricio Pochettino’s face said it all as he got off to the worst start of any Manchester United manager – or head coach – in 100 years.

The Pochettino bandwagon rolled into town with the usual fanfare of a new era, new belief, new hope; and then the wheels came off, the doors collapsed and the engine exploded. The opening quarter of an hour really was that farcical.

In that time, away to Liverpool of all places, they were 2-0 down, a player down – and down and out. If Pochettino had any uncertainty over the scale of the task ahead of him, there it was laid bare. Of course United had some mitigation. They played almost the entire game with 10 men, but teams have coped with that before and shown far more resistance and resilience. By the time United did that, it was game over. No one expected a quick fix, but come on.

Any regrets, Mauricio? Whatever the salary, he could be forgiven for having a few as he watched on. This is a far cry from being in charge of the United States and watching them roll over Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, as he did last week. If Liverpool had been more ruthless, it could have been 8-0 here.

In the end it was 4-0 – the same scoreline by which Lal Hilditch lost his first game at United, away to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926. Hilditch was a stop-gap player-manager and former central defender Pochettino may well have been tempted to bring himself on, even at the age of 54. He could barely have done worse.

Pochettino, too, can take some responsibility. Eyebrows were certainly raised when he dropped Harry Maguire – who he then had to bring on after 22 minutes – to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days. De Ligt was then at fault for the first and, arguably, the second goal.

Did the head coach start with a back three or a back four? The players seemed confused. It eventually ended up as a back five.

But this was a collective failing for United. From the top – with director of football Jason Wilcox caught on camera with his head buried in his coat – through the club and out on the pitch. Pochettino is big on building a culture. So he has to abolish the comedy and the chaos and restore credibility.

United are deep in a relegation battle. Have no doubt. Eight points after 11 games means they are currently on target for fewer than 28 points, which is a lower points-per-game total than when they were relegated in 1974.

The work needed at United is monumental. The transfer strategy has been inexplicable, with the decision being to rebuild the attack last year, the midfield this summer and wait until next year to remodel the defence. The folly of that has been exposed by the fact that United have conceded 34 goals already this season, the most in the top five European leagues.

United will argue, with justification, that Leny Yoro’s eighth-minute sending-off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity was harsh given that Alexander Isak appeared to have already lost control of the ball. But what was Yoro thinking as he bundled into the back of the forward? And what was De Ligt doing as he watched on, or lumbered on, after failing to track the run from Ronald Araújo’s ball over the top?

Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a new contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said.

“There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

“I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”

United chief executive Omar Berrada said of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his new contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

“Obviously [in 2019] I was a very young player that was eager to come to the Premier League. They had [Harry] Kane there, they had Dele Alli, Son, the chance of playing with those players in front was very attractive.”

Aston Villa have won once in their six home matches in the Premier League this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aston Villa were expecting some teething problems in 2026/27, but not being able to rely on home wins keeping them on track probably wasn’t one of them.

Villa seldom looked capable of breaking the deadlock in Saturday’s goalless draw with Sunderland. Their 2-1 win over Manchester City was their only home win in the Premier League in six attempts this season.

It’s a far cry from the general shape of Villa’s home from since Unai Emery took over as manager in the autumn of 2022. Villa Park has been the bedrock of the Emery revolution, but it’s anything but impenetrable so far this term.

Last season ended in triumph both in the fight for Champions League places and in the Europa League, but Villa’s faltering home form dates back to the start of 2026.

They won their first home match after the turn of the year but they lost their first home match for nearly four months when Everton visited Birmingham and won 1-0 in the middle of January. It was the same result against Brentford in the next home fixture and the aura, suddenly, was weakened.

A spate of midfield injuries affected those matches but Villa’s home form since New Year’s Day includes as many losses as wins in the league – six of each – and failures this season to beat Nottingham Forest (now 17th in the table), Fulham (15th) and Sunderland (19th).

Whatever that indicates about why Villa might be struggling at home, it’s clearly a problem and Emery, while positive about aspects of Villa’s play against the Black Cats, isn’t shying away from that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

One place where his team don’t come up against the exact challenges posed by some of their Premier League opponents is in the Champions League, where Villa have won two home games out of two in the league phase this season. Indeed, European competitions underpin the very notion of Villa Park as a fortress under Emery, who took Villa back into Europe ahead of the 2023/24 season.

Their last home loss in Europe was against Olympiacos in that year’s Conference League semi-finals. They won five out of six at home in the Champions League the next season, drawing the other, and won all seven of their home matches in their successful Europa League campaign in 2025/26.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

Villa’s home results in the league might have been short of their expected levels since before the summer, but there are differences between this season and last. Simply selling Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Emiliano Martinez, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Ollie Watkins fundamentally changed the picture at Villa Park.

Rogers and Tielemans were important players for breaking games open. Villa significantly outscored their expected goals value in periods of last season and goals from outside the penalty area were key.

They don’t have the same superpower this season; improving their chance creation is a must and that’s not quick or easy with any group of players, never mind a newly assembled and young team.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

There’s also a looming, inconvenient possibility that’s beginning to sustain the weight of truth. Villa Park is a three-sided stadium this season because the North Stand – ordinarily full of home supporters – is being redeveloped behind one of the goals.

The difference is intangible, indefinable, but it’s there. Even the players can’t quantify it because half of them have never played at a four-sided Villa Park, but the vacant structure behind the goal makes for an unusual atmosphere.

Emery has no interest in excuses. The Villa manager is focused on process and progress, taking every challenge for what it is and finding the answers to the questions they pose.

The North Stand redevelopment won’t be accepted as mitigation for poor home form in the dugout any more than it will in the other three stands, but Emery is no fool. He accepted after the Sunderland draw that Villa Park and the team who call it home are missing ‘something’ without the North Stand. It’s not an excuse, just another test.

Villa need to pass that test. Home results have been a hallmark of the Emery era. The manager himself has qualified for Europe every season since long before he succeeded Steven Gerrard.

One win in six is a long way short of that standard. Emery’s meticulous and measured problem-solving has been called into action once more.

Chris is a Warwickshire-based freelance football writer specialising in West Midlands football, the Premier League, the EFL and the J.League. He is the author of the High Protein Beef Paste football newsletter and owner of Aston Villa Review. He supports Coventry Sphinx.

#890. HENRY WINTER: Bruno Fernandes has been a brilliant servant, but it's time to cut the cord at Manchester United

Will Manchester United choose the 'easy option' when it comes to Bruno Fernandes' future, just as they did with handing Michael Carrick the permanent job?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United are under new management and need to be under new leadership on the field.

Bruno Fernandes has undeniably been a flickering beacon of brief hope for United in darkening times. He’s been their Player of the Year in five of the last seven seasons, risen to 19th of their greatest scorers with 113 goals, has scored 75 times (24 pens, four free-kicks) and provided 74 assists in 240 Premier League games and is the reigning Footballer of the Year. But it’s undeniably time for the club to face reality, resist the urge to extend a contract which expires next summer and build for the future.

Even taking up the year’s option (unless to increase the player’s transfer fee) would be a retrograde step. Fernandes is 32, slowing up, and not now “best in class, 10 out of 10s” to borrow Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s catchphrase. He is not the most convincing of captains, moans too much and flaps his arms like a fledgling dove attempting to leave the nest.

Fernandes would never, ever be considered one of United’s elite captains in a strong, historic field that includes Sir Bobby Charlton, Roy Keane, Bryan Robson, Steve Bruce, Roger Byrne, Nemanja Vidic and Gary Neville, amongst others.

All are different; Neville was very vocal, Charlton led by example, but were united in their total commitment.

Fernandes’ leadership qualities were brought into question when he openly criticised the tactics of Michael Carrick, effectively undermining him. That may not have been Fernandes’ intention when questioning the tactical approach against Como but it certainly didn’t help Carrick at a time when he needed players standing up to be counted, not standing up to his tactics in public. Such concerns – some of them legitimate – should have been aired in private.

It showed a lack of leadership from Fernandes, a lack of gratitude, too. Fernandes wouldn’t have been named the writers’ Footballer of the Year and the players’ Player of the Year without Carrick reviving United’s fortunes and their No. 8’s form last season.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In receiving the writers’ award in May, Fernandes eulogised about the interim head coach, praising “the amazing job” he did in guiding United into the Champions League and saying Carrick possesses the “great character to become a top manager”.

Such an endorsement from such an influential figure at the club, effectively the voice of the dressing-room, undoubtedly contributed to Ineos and the Glazers appointing Carrick to the permanent role.

Bruno’s voice is powerful. That is why it was damaging when he spoke out against Carrick’s tactics. “Lies,” was Bruno’s reaction to some of the interpretation of his words but mud stuck.

Carrick questioned individuals’ running stats – without naming Fernandes – and then dropped him for the game against Bournemouth. United need real leaders. In fairness to Fernandes, there are plenty of stories of the good work he does behind the scenes.

Who would inherit the armband in the unlikely event that Carrick’s successor, Mauricio Pochettino, was brave and looked to the future? Matthijs de Ligt, an Ajax captain at 18, would be a strong contender were it not for his back problems. Senne Lammens represents United admirably on and off the field, and was one of only two who emerged with reputation intact from Anfield.

The other was Kobbie Mainoo. It might seem a leap of faith in one so young, still only 21, but Mainoo could perform the duties until a more experienced leader was recruited by the club that once bought Keane, Bruce, Vidic etc. (All of this is a reminder of United’s need to buy leaders, powerful characters as well as good players).

Mainoo’s one of the few deserving of his place currently. He’s also an academy graduate, a local lad, and a link to great home-grown generations. Fans would love that re-affirmation of United’s identity. It would be quite a statement by Pochettino.

Mainoo has only minimal captaincy experience against Bayern Munich in 2017 (as a kid) and successfully with England Under-19s in 2023. More recently, more pertinently, Mainoo acted like a leader against Roma on November 3 when others were losing their discipline.

It’s still too early, of course, and Mainoo is still developing but he could do the honours on a temporary basis in the unlikely event that United cut the cord with Fernandes. But a recruitment department incapable of making strong decisions and buying “best in class” – they were not in the running when Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers were available in the summer - may be tempted to go for the easy option of keeping Fernandes, rather than step into a new era.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'

Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday after the Football Association found he was wrongly dismissed in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United have won their appeal against Leny Yoro’s red card at Liverpool, meaning the centre-back will not face a suspension.

Yoro will now be available for Saturday’s match against Brentford, which will be Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge at Old Trafford.

The France international was sent off in the eighth minute at Anfield for bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak. The score was 0-0 at the time but Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free kick and United went on to lose 4-0 in Pochettino’s bow.

The Argentinian voiced his displeasure with referee Sam Barrott’s decision to dismiss Yoro after the game on Sunday, calling it an “unfair situation”.

He explained: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control.” Pochettino felt that United goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have got to the ball first.

United informed the FA on Monday that they intended to appeal against the centre-back’s second red card of the season.

And an FA spokesperson said: “Leny Yoro's one-match suspension has been removed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal.

“The Manchester United player was sent off for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity during their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday 22 November.

“The independent regulatory commission's reasons for its decision will be published in due course.”

United were also aggrieved earlier this season when an “error of judgement” was made in allowing Manchester City’s winner at Old Trafford.

Defeat at Anfield left Pochettino’s side 19th in the Premier League, with just eight points from their first 11 games of the season.

Yoro is available to face Sporting in the Champions League on Wednesday while Luke Shaw has returned from injury and will travel to Portugal.

#888. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

#887. Poor Aston Villa crumble in Turkey to make it six games without a win

Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p

Emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

Though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”

Alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery said: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

Villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

Sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

That aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

Villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. They settled well in a hostile atmosphere, but allowed all their possession to drift into sterility, and the second half was just plain poor. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

The referee has allowed the game on beyond the five additional minutes, but a Harwood-Bellis loose pass stalls Villa in their own half.

They soon break out into midfield space though, but with all the time in the world Barkley’s pass was a touch behind Hemmings and Sanchez was able to get a toe to it.

Of all the venues in the Champions League where a referee might be inclined to blow his whistle as soon as possible, this might be the one so time is running out for Villa.

Lucas Torreira has taken a kick on the ankle, and he limps off to be replaced by Ilkay Gundogan, who has played just 75 minutes this season.

Villa then find some space down the left but Singo blocks Maatsen’s cross which was aimed towards Jackson.

Ross Barkley the fourth Villa player booked on the night. There will be five minutes added on, which surely does not represent all of the stoppages, but Uefa’s approach to timekeeping resembles freestyle jazz.

Villa eventually worked a position to cross the ball from that free-kick, but Lindelof’s header back into the six-yard box was too close to Cakir and the goalkeeper pounced on the ball. Time running out for Villa.

Villa have been sleepwalking to defeat throughout the second half, they have completely lost any assurance in their passing game. That was better, and Goretzka wins a free-kick in midfield which they are going to clip forward.

Buendia has been brought on for Kamara, but Hemmings shoots over when Singo was on the turf appealing for a foul not given. Villa have shown more intent in the last three minutes than the previous 30.

The goalscorer Gul is back on with a bandage around part of his face.

Things could have gone from bad to worse for Aston Villa because VAR checked for a Jackson red card for a high boot on Gul, but eventually the incident is cleared. Villa have 10 minutes plus stoppage time to salvage a result.

Mbaye with a dangerous ball into the box but he was offside in any case.

Villa undone from a corner, and the striker thrown on as a substitute has scored the game’s opening goal. Gul appears to have hurt himself in the process, he took a kick in the face from Jackson when planting his head on the ball. Villa lost the first contact at the near-post and from there it was a mess. Gul receiving treatment with blood streaming down his face.

The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p

Tyrone Mings defends well but he cannot prevent Galatasaray winning another second-half corner.

Galatasaray with a double change: Sara and Ugochukwu on for Batrakov and Lemina.

Emery responds in kind: Hemmings and Barkley on for Manzambi and McGinn.

Aston Villa struggling to find any rhythm after another stoppage in the game, but Galatasaray are enjoying more of the territory. Nicolas Jackson has been a revelation this season but has been underwhelming in the second half.

Now Gortetzka is waved on by the referee, who made Villa wait because Gomes took too long to walk off the pitch. Suzuki commands his box in the air once again to climb a high ball launched into the mixer.

Alysson and Gomes are the players coming off for Mbaye and Goretzka, but the German midfielder has been to wait on the touchline by the referee much to Emery’s Fury. Gomes has already gone off, so Villa are down to 10. Bizarre officiating, not sure I can recall seeing that.

Now Galatasaray have a corner! But Villa clear at the near post.

Villa floundering and under pressure for the first time in the game, Mbaye and Goretzka are about to be introduced by Emery.

Galatasaray have a free-kick in a crossing position left of centre, but Akgun’s delivery floated over everyone in the box and Torreira is then penalised for a foul on Manzambi.

Galatasaray have made a change in their attack, with a more orthodox striker in Gul replaces Elmali, so Yilmaz moves out to the left. Torreira wins a foul in midfield, but Gomes and Kamara were convinced they had won the ball cleanly.

That aggro has given Galatasaray a lift and the noise is now increasing.

Villa have slightly lost their way in the last 10 minutes, they are not passing the ball with their early fluency and appear caught between holding what they have or pushing on for a goal. Maatsen the latest player guilty of a cheap giveaway.

Akgun reacts with fury after he is tripped on the sly by Alysson to stop a break away, and they square up to each other. Both players have been booked, so there have been five yellow cards so far.

Suzuki does well to claim a cross but he caught Elmali who stays down in the penalty area to receive some treatment. A little bit of needle in the game is welcome because neither team is creating much.

Galatasaray waste a corner, and then Villa spring a counter-attack despite Maatsen’s initial poor pass. Sanchez crashed into a challenge on Alysson, before McGinn returns the favour with interest on Batrakov. McGinn is booked for the tackle, Batrakov for his reaction. The Galatasaray player kicked out slightly after he was bodied by the Villa man. Both benches were up, but no further punishement for either player.

Jackson nods the ball down into a dangerous area but Bardakci clears for Galatasaray. Villa continue to dominate possession, Galatasaray keep going long towards Yilmaz to no avail. They are feeling the absence of Osimhen.

Very messy defending from Galatasaray and there are vociferous appeals for a Villa penalty after a lunging challenge in the box, but the referee and VAR decide there is nothing in it. The layer of sand under the top surface of the pitch is becoming increasingly visible as the game goes on.

No changes from either manager at half-time.

Unai Emery will be fairly satisfied with that first-half performance.

In a match of few chances, Villa have frustrated the home team and defended resolutely in the rare occasions Galatasaray have applied pressure.

The pitch is slowing the game down which is helping Villa. There was a weird booking for Nicolas Jackson late in the half so it would be no surprise to see him taken off by Emery either at half-time or very early in the second.

A controlled and composed 45 minutes from Villa, but in truth Galatasaray have put them under very little pressure. McGinn, Manzambi and Jackson have produced some smooth flicks and touches, but there has been a lack of devastation in the final third. That has been the missing element for Villa so far. For all the talk of the atmosphere, they should be beating this team.

Nicolas Jackson has been booked, and Alysson loses the ball cheaply to put Galatasaray away on the counter-attack. Mings is up early to head the corner away. The home team continue to look pretty toothless.

Elmali’s cross from the Galatasaray left is woefully overhit and Suzuki claims, but it was a poor pass from Harwood-Bellis that instigated the attack. Villa soon restore order with a spell of possession.

Unsurprisingly, the best pass of the match so far has come from Zion Suzuki.

The Villa goalkeeper has just pinged a pearler over 40 odd yards to Alysson on the right wing.

Galatasaray find some joy with quick switches of play with Villa’s defensive shape quite narrow, but Akgun’s chipped cross was overhit.

Joao Gomes then takes an extra touch inside his own box, but moves the ball on before he is caught in possession.

Torreira than clatters Gomes, not his first foul on the night, but somehow he escapes a booking.

McGinn is picking up some midfield positions that are hard for Galatasaray to pick up, but a couple of Hollywood passes from there have not come off.

Better attacking play from the home team, but Mings was well positioned to head clear a deflected cross.

For a moment it looks as if Manzambi had missed a glorious chance but the flag belatedly went up for offside against Jackson who collected the ball wide right when well ahead of the play.

Villa are doing a very good job of frustrating both the Galatasaray players and their supporters so far.

They are slowing the game down and producing some neat interplay in advanced positions.

Johan Manzambi, in particular, is covering a lot of ground.

Suzuku rushes off his line to sweep up a through ball, but Alysson had also tracked a run all the way. Singo passes forward quickly but Galatasaray’s playmaker Batrakov cannot put the ball under his spell.

John McGinn with a chance to deliver a free-kick from a crossing position, but Galatasaray win the header at the back post. Villa continue to be comfortable in the game, without really working the goalkeeper Cakir. The home crowd are restless, Galatasaray have yet to muster a menacing attacking.

Villa moving the ball well inside Galatasaray’s half with some neat interplay between Manzambi and Jackson when they are in close proximity, but there is no telling pass or shot at the end of the move.

Lovely turn from John McGinn between the lines but Galatasaray’s defender Bardakci intercepted his through ball. Manzambi started wide left on the team sheet, but Maatsen’s runs forward are allowing the Swiss to play in a narrower position.

Akgun wins a free-kick for Galatasaray, who have grown into the contest in the last few minutes. Torreira and Batrakov swapping positions in midfield, and Singo is an impressive player at right-back. The delivery from the free-kick is poor though.

Galatasaray did beat Liverpool twice in this competition last season so cannot be taken lightly tonight.

The pitch does appear to be cutting up a bit in some areas already.

Jackson perhaps unfortunate not be awarded a foul in the left corner, but this has been a bright start by Villa.

Their front players Manazmbi, Alysson and Jackson all combined in a one-touch move after Suzuki played long before the Villa striker was flagged offside.

Lovely pass from Zion Suzuki inside the opening minute, picking out Harwood-Bellis who was free down the right. He found Manzambi unmarked in the middle before Maatsen’s progress down the left was halted. Villa enjoy drawing a press, so it could suit them if the home team are aggressive.

Villa get the game under way, and from the aerial view you can see the seams between patches of the pitch.

A cacophony of hoots, howls and whistles will greet the Villa players, and the same will be true of their every touch of the ball. Aleksey Batrakov, likely to play in behind Yilmaz for the home team, has been identified as Galatasaray’s potential danger man.

Alejandro Garnacho has now been left out of the Villa squad for four games in a row.

He trained at Bodymoor Heath on Monday so does not appear to be injured.

It is looking pretty bleak for the Chelsea loanee, and the comparisons with Liverpool’s Harvey Elliott last season are impossible to escape.

Villa have made a solid start on their return to the Champions League, winning three and losing one.

Victory here would give them a fine chance of progress to the knock-out stages, and provide Unai Emery with some insurance.

Villa face a daunting pair of home games against Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund in their next two league phase matches.

No problems, no. We must play in all pitches, even synthetic we play in the Champions League. It’s not perfect but it is good enough to play football.

Very competitive [on Galatasaray], they are at home so, so intense with their supporters.

We must play focused, together, try and set our game plan as much as possible. We must try and dominate in the way we must build the team.

Six months after the glory of winning the Europa League final in Istanbul, Aston Villa are back on the banks of the Bosphorus.

A potentially tricky match awaits against the Turkish champions, with much of the pre-match scrutiny on the state of the pitch.

Villa were unable to train on Rams Park on Monday as the club is undertaking repair work to the surface.

A positive result and no injuries would represent a great evening for Unai Emery.

Emery appears to be using the versatile Manzambi in a wide left starting position with McGinn in the middle in front of Gomes and Kamara. Mings for Pau Torres is surely all about rotation, with Villa going to Ipswich on Tuesday night. Harwood-Bellis could play at right-back in a similar set-up to the one Villa deployed at Old Trafford.

Lucas Torreira was signed by Arsenal in 2018, Unai Emery’s first summer as head coach. Gundogan has not played many minutes at all this season, but is back on the bench. Osimhen and Leao missing a significant chunk of the season is a major disappointment.

Galatasaray XI: Cakir, Singo, Sanchez, Bardakci, Jakobs, Torreira, Lemina, Elmali, Akgun, Batrakov, Baris Yilmaz

In come Lindelof, Mings, Gomes and McGinn for Wan-Bissaka, Torres, Goretezka and Buendia.

Aston Villa supporters have happy memories of Istanbul after May’s Europa League final, and they return to face Galatasaray this evening in a fixture which could forecast their Champions League prospects.

It has been par for the course for Unai Emery’s team in Europe so far, with victories over Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking and a defeat at Barcelona aligning with the form book.

Nine points from 12 leaves them inside the top eight at the halfway stage of the league phase, but tougher challenges are ahead with PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come after tonight’s game.

Since a statement victory over Manchester City, it has been a frustrating time for Villa either side of the international break. They were dumped out of the League Cup by Bournemouth, were second-best in a home draw with Fulham, threw away a pair of two-goal leads at Old Trafford, and were held by Sunderland at the weekend.

Though Villa put six past Galatasaray’s city rivals Fenerbahce at Villa Park, away games against Turkish opposition can be different beasts, as Liverpool discovered in the last round of Champions League matches.

Galatasaray’s two major attacking threats, Victor Osimhen and Rafael Leão, are both absent with injuries. Davinson Sanchez and Lucas Torreira are former Premier League players in their squad. Galatasaray have won two of four Champions League games, losing to Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon, but they are top of the Turkish Super Lig.

Villa will be without right-back Matty Cash owing to a concussion sustained during the international break with Poland, but will hope to have Victor Lindelof available again after he missed the Sunderland draw with illness.

Emery’s team were unable to train at Rams Park yesterday in order to give a troublesome pitch maximum recovery time after emergency renovation work.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”

Arsenal's January transfer plans have been thrown into chaos following an anterior cruciate ligament injury.

The Gunners strengthened over the summer to bring in Ezri Konsa and Bruno Guimaraes in defence and midfield respectively, but with Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli and Leandro Trossard all leaving in attack, only Christos Tzolis came into replace the trio.

With Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta needing reinforcements in attack, the window transfer window would have seen the Gunners have a free run at some of their bigger targets – until now.

Over the weekend, Paris Saint-Germain forward Desire Doue was stretchered off against Nice with a suspected ACL rupture.

This is the second time that a PSG attacker has suffered a season-ending injury in the past few weeks, with Khvicha Kvaratskhelia also damaging his ACL against Barcelona in the Champions League earlier this season.

The double-blow leaves the European champions light in attack, with Ousmane Dembele the only remaining recognised senior forward from the past two Champions League-winning campaigns, and the 2025 Ballon d'Or winner supplemented by the likes of Mika Godts, Magnes Akliouche and the 2026 World Cup final scorer, Ferran Torres.

And while much of this has very little to do with the team that PSG beat in last year's Champions League final, Arsenal, both sides have had similar targets on their radar over the past 18 months.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Godts was admired by Arteta before his switch to Ligue 1, as was Torres – while Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi is thought to be a big target in attack this winter for the Gunners, as per TEAMtalk, along with Antonio Nusa.

Julian Alvarez is another big-name forward that both PSG and Arsenal were vying for in the summer, with the Argentine ruling out a move to anywhere other than Barcelona.

January will be a difficult time in N5 for business as it is, given their approach over the summer.

The champions were blown out of the water for a move for Morgan Rogers, valuing him at over £20 million less than what he moved for, while a deal for Bradley Barcola remained a non-starter due to the Frenchman's extortionate price tag.

If Arteta is to bring in a new face midseason, the Gunners may have to break the bank – and with PSG competing with them, that may just complicate things far more than expected.

Arsenal face Borussia Dortmund as Champions League action resumes this week.
