#855. IFA 'positive' over upgrades needed for World Cup

Windsor Park would require 5,000 additional seats to host games at the 2035 World Cup

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt said the organisation is "still working through" plans with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that."

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but plans for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government said it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt said that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

"We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here."

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms

Plans to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a new generation".

"I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she said.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in New Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

"That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general."

Exactly how much Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) headroom do Manchester United have to back Mauricio Pochettino in the January transfer window?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has barely unpacked his bags at Old Trafford, but it's already abundantly clear Manchester United need to back their new head coach in January.

Following a disappointing start to the campaign and the arrival of a new regulatory era in English football, the club’s latest financial results offer a clear picture as to how much room INEOS actually have to manoeuvre.

Man United’s most recent full-year accounts, covering the 12-month period to 30 June, 2026, which were published in September, paints a picture of cost-cutting paired with historically strong commercial standing.

Despite having no European football last season, Man United posted record revenue of £677.6 million while trimming wages for a third consecutive year to £302.0m.

Although previous recruitment pushed player amortisation to £211.8m and left a net loss of £43.0m after finance costs, £47.0m in player-sale profits kept the underlying business moving forward.

Even more telling are Man United’s first-quarter results for 2026/27, released on November 19.

With Champions League football back at Old Trafford, quarterly revenue rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m, and the club are predicted to earn £740m and £760m annually.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Quarterly player amortisation fell by almost 15 per cent following summer exits and Casemiro’s contract expiry, while another £20.7m was banked in player-disposal profits.

This summer, the Premier League replaced Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) with its new Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) system. Under SCR, clubs’ on-pitch spending - which comprises first-team player and head coach wages, transfer amortisation, and agent fees, while excluding non-playing staff, academy and women’s team costs - is capped at 85 per cent of football revenue plus net profit on player sales.

There is even a 30 per cent multi-year buffer up to a 115 per cent ‘Red Threshold’ before points deductions apply. However, because Man United are competing in the Champions League, they must simultaneously adhere to UEFA’s stricter 70 per cent squad cost limit ahead of the March 1 compliance checkpoint.

Therefore, Pochettino has far more breathing room in the transfer market than naysayers might suggest.

Taking the £750m midpoint of Man United’s expected 2026/27 revenue and adding roughly £45m - which is an average of player-trading profits over recent years - that gives an adjusted revenue figure of £795m.

Under the Premier League’s 85 per cent threshold, Man United could carry £675.8m in annual squad costs. Under UEFA’s tighter 70 per cent ceiling, their limit sits at £556.5m.

Remove non-playing staff from total wages and Man United’s first-team player and coaching bill sits near £255m. Add £186.4m in annualised amortisation and roughly £35m in agents’ fees, and total squad costs land around £476.4m - roughly 60 per cent of adjusted revenue.

That leaves roughly £80m in annual squad-cost headroom beneath UEFA’s 70 per cent cap - and nearly £200m domestically.

This means Man United could comfortably sanction £120m to £150m in winter transfer spending. That said, their borrowing position and existing credit facility could yet prove to be a handbrake on any January rebuild, but from a purely regulatory standpoint, Man United's transfer expenditure picture is a rosy one.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#853. 'Our Super Bowl moment' - what can WSL learn from booming US league?

Kansas City Current, who were formed in 2020, won this year's National Women's Soccer League championship

"It's turning into our Super Bowl moment."

Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.

The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (Â£229).

Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.

Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.

It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.

Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.

So what is behind the explosion in popularity?

And what can the Women's Super League learn from it?

The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.

The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.

"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.

"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."

While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.

The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.

There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.

As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.

Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.

Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.

"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.

"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."

It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.

But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.

"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.

"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."

Bespoke women's football stadiums? Why US sides are making the move

Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built Â£80m women's stadium

Washington Spirit's Trinity Rodman benefited from a NWSL decision in December 2025 to lift the league's salary cap for a 'High Impact Player'

Fans of both the NWSL and the WSL are spoiled when it comes to talent.

Most of the US national team play their club football at home, with the likes of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Rose Lavelle household names.

International stars such as Malawi's Temwa Chawinga at Kansas City, who came 10th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings, and former Chelsea striker Sam Kerr further enhance the league's quality.

"Where it starts is the product on the pitch," says Jones Simmer. "The quality of football has to be incredible and we have the best players in the world.

"And they are incredibly engaging with our fans. For so many supporters, their entry point to the league is they care about a particular player."

Provided the standard of competition is present, Jones Simmer says fans will return - and her confidence is backed up by the numbers.

In 2026, the average gate for an NWSL match has been more than 11,000 - only Arsenal in the WSL consistently receive a higher attendance than that, albeit the US is almost five times more populous than the UK.

On Thursday, the final few tickets for the NWSL's showpiece were retailing at $300 on ticket site Viagogo, with Jones Simmer suggesting resale tickets could be purchased at six times market value in advance of the match.

As London City and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang put it: "The answer could not be clearer that there is an audience for the women's game."

"It's our job to hook fans by making sure they have a great experience watching a game in a venue and that's about the quality of the product," Jones Simmer adds.

"Once folks have that experience, it's a really easy yes to tune in again."

Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma

Not that quality is an issue in the WSL where high-class footballers abound. Take Putellas, goal machine Khadija Shaw and most of England's double European Championship-winning squad for example.

American stars such as Alyssa Thompson and Naomi Girma at Chelsea, and Manchester City's Sam Coffey, have also swapped the US for the WSL in the past two years.

Broadcaster Oatley, who has been covering women's football since the 2005 World Cup, is keen for such players to be more visible off the pitch.

"I would love to see WSL players on mainstream TV shows, podcasts, social media platforms, not just on women's football programmes where the audience already knows everything about them," she says.

"It would not be for everyone, but for those who are comfortable, who have the biggest personalities, I think we could use that much more to grow our audience."

Oatley has been covering NWSL games for the past four seasons and she believes US clubs have mastered putting on events.

"When you're trying to promote a product in sport, you can't guarantee the team is going to play well and win," she says.

"But you can ensure the people who come to the game have a great experience.

"I love the enthusiasm, the positivity, the vibe of 'let's make this big'. It's a brilliant experience."

It is a balance the WSL wrestles with. With attendances plateauing this season, questions have arisen around its target audience and whether to market matches such as the north London derby between Tottenham and Arsenal as a rivalry or a family-friendly event.

Oatley's perspective is that it ought to be both, while recognising the different challenges in this country.

"I didn't understand that criticism," she says, "because they weren't saying: 'Only come to this game if you're a family'. It was being promoted all round.

"I don't think it's one size fits all marketing wise - the main thing is awareness."

The NWSL Fan Fest at The Wharf in Washington DC was part of a series of events around the championship game on Saturday

It is a challenge the NWSL has embraced, and seen attendances rise accordingly.

"We want to ensure that we provided a big enough tent where everyone can feel welcome and included, whether they're there for the rivalries and the competitive tactics, or they're experiencing it for the first time," says Jones Simmer.

"To grow the sport, all fans need to be able to come to an NWSL game and have a great experience."

This season, league finalists Current and Spirit played at a remarkable 17 different times between them, reflecting the four timezones and vast nature of the USA.

It is all part of the country's sporting landscape, but given the WSL's continued conundrum about fixture scheduling, it is interesting that NWSL supporters manage to find the matches regardless.

"I have a lot of sympathy with schedulers because men's football got there first," Oatley says.

"Maybe the solution is deciding certain time slots are for women's football and sticking with them."

It does not appear the growth in the NWSL will slow down any time soon.

The Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer will feature the USA as one of the favourites and women's soccer will feature at the Olympic Games in Los Angeles in 2028.

The US will also host the 2031 Women's World Cup.

"It is amazing how the NWSL is cracking into culture," Jones Simmer says.

"We get excited about these catalytic opportunities to expand the community engagement, awareness and relevance of the NWSL."

#852. What's going on with the polar vortex?

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

#851. Can returning Beattie and Haughey make an impact?

Beattie won the last of her 13 caps last year while the uncapped Haughey was last called into the senior squad in 2021

Michael McArdle has decided the upcoming friendly double-header against Greece is the perfect time to bring back Kerry Beattie and Ella Haughey from the international wilderness.

Glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron is also in under McArdle for the first time after a lengthily absence, but the Glentoran midfielder would likely have been included sooner if not for a spell on the sidelines through injury.

Beattie won her last cap a year ago while Haughey will hope to make a senior debut in one of the two games against Greece at Inver Park after she was an unused substitute in friendlies against England and Scotland in her sole call up in 2021.

The inclusion of both players, who have been in good form at their clubs, shows McArdle is willing to keep the door open for a return to the international squad if players are performing at club level.

Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies

Portsmouth striker Beattie has been in and out of squads since her debut in 2021.

The 24-year-old has four goals in 13 caps, the last of which she won against Iceland in the Nations League play-off a year ago.

A prolific forward during two spells at Glentoran, she has struggled for consistency in moves across to Scotland with the likes of Glasgow City, Hearts and Aberdeen.

She left the Dons in the summer and consulted with McArdle when deciding upon her next move, before joining WSL 2 side Portsmouth.

Beattie has eight goals in all competitions for a Pompey side languishing at the bottom of the table and McArdle is pleased she has settled in well.

"Kerry had spells at Hearts and Aberdeen and for whatever reason it didn't quite work out at both, she had good spells but not a consistent run to express herself," McArdle said.

"The move to Portsmouth, I was delighted she reached out to me for some advice, it's an alignment for her and it's been a great move on and off the pitch. It's allowed her to enjoy herself but also play 90 minutes and be that focal point striker.

"She will have been disappointed not to make the squad for the [World Cup] play-off [against Portugal] with her form but she worked hard and she's back in, I'm delighted for her."

Beattie faces stiff competition for the starting striker role from the likes of returning captain Simone Magill and Kess Elmore, who impressed in the last camp and scored against Portugal, but she should receive some minutes across the two games and will be keen to grasp her chance to make an impact.

Left-back Haughey was called up to the senior squad as a 16-year-old under Kenny Shiels, but did not feature

West Brom defender Haughey's last involvement with NI came when she represented the under-19s in 2023.

A Lisburn Rangers player when Kenny Shiels included her in the senior squad as a 16-year-old, Haughey then moved to Nottingham Forest before settling at the Baggies, who play in the National League.

The left-back, 22, has been a regular this season for the club in the third tier and combines playing with her university studies.

Left-back has been a problem position for NI which McArdle has been trying to address as demonstrated by him bringing in Lucy-Jayne Grant in the last camp and Haughey for this window to allow Rebecca Holloway to play as a central defender.

Haughey will be competing with Grant to fill that full-back role on the left side and McArdle believes she is more than capable of doing so having tried to bring her back into the squad earlier in his reign.

"Ella's been at West Brom for a few years now. She has real potential, strong, athletic potential. We tried to call her up sooner but there were some challenges," he explained.

"She's probably been one of their top performers and one of the top performers in the league. Delighted she's earned this opportunity and hopefully she can make her debut and achieve her first cap."

McArdle has made a concerted to continue to widen the player pool available to him as he aims to build depth ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, but if Beattie and Haughey catch the eye it will show that giving chances to those previously involved under different managers could be another possibility.

#850. Morocco FA filed challenge against Cas arbitrator less than hour before Afcon final verdict

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Morocco filed a challenge against of the judicial panel within an hour prior to Senegal’s appeal being officially upheld

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Morocco’s federation submitted a last-minute challenge to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) against a member of the judicial panel before Senegal saw their Africa Cup of Nations appeal upheld, restoring them as 2025 champions.

Senegal contested the Confederation of African Football's (Caf) decision to declare Morocco champions after the team staged an injury-time walk-off in protest to a penalty awarded against them, and were successful in their appeal as Cas, sport’s highest court, found that referee Jean-Jacques Ndala “did not commit any error of law” when he decided to resume the match.

The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) responded to Tuesday’s verdict by questioning “the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process”, a complaint surrounding an alleged phone call involving Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall and arbitrator Ulrich Haas.

The Independent understands that Cas received a challenge against Haas by the FRMF within one hour prior to the decision being announced. This formally came several hours after media reports stated it had already been filed.

The Icas Challenge Commission reviewed the FRMF’s challenge but found there was not enough evidence at the time to delay the verdict’s announcement.

Sources indicate that Haas strongly denies any direct contact at any moment with the Senegalese federation or any parties involved throughout the arbitration process, while the FSF also vehemently refuted the allegations as “fake news”.

The FRMF has vowed to pursue further legal action to appeal the verdict.

A statement read: “The Royal Moroccan Football Federation expresses its surprise and protest at the failure to take into account its demand to arrange the necessary legal consequences for practices that would compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration procedure, especially what has been confirmed regarding communication between the German referee Ulrich Haas and the president of the Senegalese Football Federation, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

“The Royal Moroccan Football Federation also notes that the decision did not take into account the approach recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (Ifab) and Fifa, regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee’s permission, and the resulting disciplinary responsibilities and penalties.

“Accordingly, the Royal Moroccan Football Federation confirms its intention to pursue all available legal avenues to appeal the decision of the Court of Arbitration for Sport.”

Newcastle United and head coach Matthias Jaissle could reunite with a former striker, according to reports

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Newcastle are being tipped to solve their goalscoring issues this winter with a move to bring Ivan Toney back to St James’ Park.

It is a transfer which would reunite the England international with former boss Matthias Jaissle, with whom he worked at current club Al-Ahli.

Finding the back of the net has proved a major headache for Jaissle since taking the reins on Tyneside and following a summer exodus that stripped the Magpies of their spine, none of Newcastle’s current central striking options have managed to nail down a starting spot in his team.

Will Osula and Yoane Wissa have mustered just a single league goal apiece so far this campaign, while Matias Fernandez-Pardo is still waiting to open his account. Without a reliable penalty-box presence, Jaissle’s side have lacked a cutting edge in the final third.

Toney thrived under Jaissle during their time together in Saudi Arabia. The former Brentford frontman has been expectedly prolific in the Middle East, netting 87 times in 110 appearances across all competitions.

Any transfer negotiations may even be smoothed over by shared ownership links, as both Al-Ahli and Newcastle are majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Despite his form in the Saudi Pro League, Toney has slipped down the international pecking order and missed out on recent England squads, a setback that is expected to spark a push for a Premier League return in the New Year.

Speaking on the Everything is Black and White Podcast, The Chronicle’s chief Newcastle reporter Lee Ryder suggested the 30-year-old will be chomping at the bit to head back to English football.

A switch to St James’ Park would see Toney return to the club he departed almost a decade ago. Newcastle originally signed the striker from Northampton Town over in 2015, but made just two Premier League outings before being sent out on a series of loans. Spells at Barnsley, Shrewsbury, Scunthorpe and Wigan followed, before he was eventually sold to Peterborough United in 2018.

Having since proved his top-flight pedigree at Brentford, Toney would bring additional physicality and an aptitude for finishing that Newcastle are presently missing.

#846. Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir

Caroline Weir says it is "amazing" that Scotland will host the World Cup finals

Scotland captain Caroline Weir says hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup along with England, Northern Ireland and Wales will usher in "an amazing decade of excitement" for the game in her homeland.

World governing body Fifa confirmed on Monday that the United Kingdom will host a football World Cup for the first time since England won the men's tournament on home soil in 1966.

Scotland's national stadium at Hampden Park in Glasgow and Hibernian's Easter Road Stadium in Leith are among 19 venues chosen for the 39-day competition involving 48 teams.

At the age of 31 now, Weir would have to show unusual longevity to still be playing at that point, but she still considers it "amazing news, not just for young players that hope to play there but for us, in this period in between, to develop the women's game in Scotland - and to push it.

"So I think it's amazing news and I think it's going to be an amazing decade of excitement leading into this World Cup".

Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup

Big wins as Celtic, Rangers, City & Hearts progress

The Lyon midfielder has already played for Scotland the only time they have so far qualified for a World Cup finals - in 2019.

"As a young, aspiring footballer watching football on TV growing up, for your home country to actually host a tournament itself, and the World Cup itself, the biggest tournament in football, is the most amazing thing," Weir said.

"So, if I was a 10 or 11 year old girl now, I would be thinking this is the best news ever and I'm going to work and practice and hope that, one day, I am representing Scotland in a home nations tournament playing at Hampden Park in a World Cup for Scotland.

"I don't think it gets any bigger or better than that."

Angie Hind, Scotland Under-23 head coach and Scottish FA player pathway manager, also thinks it will prove inspirational to the young players under her charge.

"If you think of the young players who are involved in our pathway right now, from 13 years old right through the 23s that I take, that's the future," the former Scotland midfielder told BBC Scotland.

"That's very much those players who will be pulling on a Scotland jersey when we are part of that World Cup."

Hind pointed out that it "fits perfectly" with Project 2035, announced this month by SFA and Scottish government, designed to boost the long-term growth of the girls and women's game.

For SFA head of women's and girls football Shirley Martin, it is a "tremendous milestone" considering holding a World Cup had been such "a game changer" for previous hosts.

"Ten years ago, a home World Cup have felt like a dream and now it's happening," she told BBC Radio 5 live. "I think it shows how far women's football has come."

Martin pointed out that the SFA hopes to "double our participation over that time" as well as improving coaching, referees, clubs and facilities - and are already doing so.

However, she admitted: "The one thing we need to do is increase the crowds that come to matches."

#845. Senegal re-crowned Afcon champions after appeal upheld

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Senegal were stripped of their Afcon title for staging a walk-off and Morocco will appeal the latest ruling

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Senegal have been re-crowned the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) unanimously upheld their appeal against the decision to strip them of their title on Tuesday.

Senegal contested Confederation of African Football's (Caf) decision to declare Morocco champions, which wiped the Teranga Lions’ title from the records despite victory in January’s Afcon final 1-0 after extra time in Rabat.

The final was fraught with controversy after Senegal staged a walk-off in protest to a penalty was awarded against them in the dying stages of normal time, with players ordered into the dressing room by manager Pape Thiaw, where they remained for 14 minutes.

Play was eventually resumed before Morocco’s Brahim Diaz missed the spot-kick, sailing a tame ‘Panenka’ effort into the arms of Edouard Mendy. Senegal went on to win the match in extra time through Pape Gueye.

However, they were stripped of the title two months later after Caf’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited ⁠the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 ​victory to ⁠Morocco.

Senegal quickly followed with an appeal to sport's highest court, Cas, which was lodged on 25 March and have now successfully fought their case to be reinstated as champions, with the original 1-0 result restored.

The three-man Cas ‌panel, presided over by French sports law ​expert Gerald Simon with assistance from ‌Italian international law professor ⁠Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based ⁠attorney Ulrich Haas, ‌unanimously found that referee Jean-Jacques Ndala “did not commit any error of law”, said Cas secretary general Matthieu Reeb.

Ndala’s decision to resume the match after Senegal’s walk-off fell within his sole authority and was therefore covered by the “field of play” doctrine, something Morocco’s federation argued was not the case.

The court published its reasoning in a press release issued on Tuesday afternoon, which read: “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.

“In the panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the referee’s decision were limited to the pitch.”

The panel clarified that Articles 82 and 84 of Caf’s tournament regulations, cited in the Moroccan federation’s appeal, apply only to determining match results if team conduct forces a referee to permanently call off a game, and were therefore not applicable in this instance.

"In conclusion, the panel considers that in resuming the match, the referee did not err in law," a court press release added.

“The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Cas noted that disciplinary action has already been taken against then-Senegal boss Thiaw, the Senegalese federation and certain players following separate proceedings by Caf.

Senegal took to social media to celebrate the verdict, posting a picture of the team lifting the trophy with the caption, “Encore et toujours champions d’Afrique” - which translates to, “Champions of Africa, once again and always”.

“The Senegalese Football Federation welcomes this sentence with deep satisfaction,” a federation statement read.

“Far from consecrating the preeminence of one party over another, this decision affirms above all the triumph of sporting fairness and recalls a cardinal principle: the truth of a match is established exclusively on the field, under the protection of sports law.

“On this solemn occasion, the FSF wishes to express its deep gratitude to the Lions of Teranga and their management, to its lawyers and advisors, to the President of the Republic and the Senegalese Government for their support, as well as to all supporters, both in Senegal and in the diaspora.”

The Moroccan federation (FRMF) released a statement confirming its intention to “pursue all available legal avenues” to appeal the decision.

The federation alleged there had been “communication” between a member of the Cas panel and the president of the Senegalese federation 48 hours before the decision was issued.

The FRMF said these practices would “compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration procedure”.

Cas has been contacted for comment regarding this allegation.

The FRMF added that the decision “did not take into account the approach recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (IFAB) and Fifa, regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee’s permission, and the resulting disciplinary responsibilities and penalties”.

Cas initially promised a decision within days of the 8 October in-person hearing in Lausanne but then decided to issue a complete ruling, including legal grounds, known as a Cas Award - a process that requires several weeks.

Cas Awards hold the same value as a national court judgement, enforceable in accordance with the New York Convention on the Recognition ‌and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards.

The full Cas Award will be published in due course.

#844. SFA leads tributes to former president Peat

Former Scottish FA president George Peat has died at the age of 86.

The former Airdrieonians and Stenhousemuir director spent four years in the role, taking over from John McBeth in 2007.

He oversaw the appointments of Scotland managers George Burley and Craig Levein and commissioned former first minister Henry McLeish to conduct a review of Scottish football.

Peat was also at the helm when Scottish referees opted to take strike action in November 2010.

"George loved his football and was renowned as a forthright personality and formidable negotiator but behind that imposing exterior lay a sharp wit and a glint in his eye," said current SFA president Mike Mulraney.

"He cared deeply about the national game and his beloved Airdrieonians.

"George was also passionate about the modernisation of the association and commissioned the McLeish Review of Scottish football as one of his first acts as president.

"He was a regular visitor to Hampden, even as his health deteriorated, and will be sadly missed by his friends and former colleagues at the Scottish FA and across the game."

#842. Liverpool’s Florian Wirtz enjoying and relishing uptick in form

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Wirtz has struggled to settle in England since making the switch from Bayer Leverkusen but feels he his hitting form at a good time for the Reds

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Florian Wirtz admitted he has been unhappy with some of his performances for Liverpool but he is now enjoying being in his best run of form since joining the club.

The Germany playmaker’s performances have been intensely scrutinised since his £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen two summers ago and, after an underwhelming first season in a campaign where the whole team struggled, he has started to kick into gear.

He has scored five times and contributed two assists in his last four appearances for club and country and the smile is back on his face.

“In the last few games I got a lot of goal contributions and I think you could say that I am in the best form since I arrived,” he said ahead of the Champions League game against Club Brugge in Belgium.

“To be honest, I cannot really say that I have changed much. I think that I have become a bit better on a physical level, that is the only reason I could explain it.

“But I also started to know better English football and the league and I am feeling very good. I am enjoying my football at Liverpool. I am happy it is going like this at the moment.

“I have heard a lot of people talking about me smiling or that I don’t smile that much. Maybe that is only because the people don’t really know me. Normally I am a very positive guy.

“It’s just when I am on the pitch I try and bring out my best performances and be as focused as I can be. Maybe that is sometimes why it looks like I don’t smile so much, but I don’t think that is a thing you have to be concerned about.

“It’s mainly a thing that goes on in my own head. It’s not about the people who talk about me. It’s the goals I set myself and the performances I want to show for myself.

“I always believed in myself. I knew my qualities and I know them now.

“Of course, there were days where I wasn’t happy with myself but I still believe it makes no sense to put too much pressure on yourself as that doesn’t help to get to where you want.

“I just believed in myself so I wasn’t too annoyed. But now I can only speak about the time I am having now and I’m really enjoying it.”

After a run one goal in 17 club appearances stretching back to May, the 23-year-old has scored in back-to-back matches and he created 10 chances in Sunday’s win against Manchester United, including an assist for Victor Munoz’s goal.

Wirtz added: “I would say my priority is that the club and the team is successful, that’s the main thing in my head.

“I know that offensive players get checked by numbers and I’m always trying to use my opportunities when I have them but, in the end, for me it’s just about the success of the team.

“I’m not going into a game and trying to be the player who has scored the most goals or something. If I see a team-mate in a better position I give them the ball and I hope they also do that with me.”

#841. 'I persuaded my club to give me a job as a content creator'

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

He's a content creator for Bolton Wanderers FC, he comes up with new ideas for social media, filming videos and posts them onto official pages. The aim is to encourage people to follow the club.

There are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator

While it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities."

Jacob says salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

Find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

#840. The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

#838. Howard Webb backs process of Leny Yoro red card despite successful appeal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Howard Webb said the call was ‘certainly not clearly wrong’ in comments recorded before the FA lifted Yoro’s suspension

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Referees’ chief Howard Webb has voiced his support for the decision-making behind Leny Yoro’s red card against Liverpool, despite his one-match suspension being lifted by the FA.

Yoro was sent off for fouling Alexander Isak as the Swede ran towards the goal just eight minutes into Manchester United’s 4-0 defeat to Liverpool on Sunday.

Referee Sam Barrott adjudged it to be a denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity, but United appealed for wrongful dismissal and had their appeal upheld by the FA, meaning the French defender is free to feature in United’s home game against Brentford this Saturday.

The FA said the written reasons for removing the suspension would be published in due course.

Pro Ref’s chief refereeing officer Webb, however, backed the decision to dismiss the 21-year-old, saying the call was “certainly not clearly wrong”.

Liverpool scored their opening goal directly from the free-kick awarded for Yoro’s challenge and scored a further three without reply in a torrid start to Mauricio Pochettino’s tenure as United manager.

Webb discussed the incident with former Liverpool and United striker Michael Owen in the latest edition of Match Officials: Mic’d Up, which aired on Tuesday evening but was recorded before the FA confirmed Yoro’s suspension had been removed.

“The reason we’re talking about it is the fourth consideration (in DOGSO decisions), that’s control or likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball,” Webb said.

“Isak’s got control of the ball, he’s got possession, he’s got the touch, he knocks it past Yoro. He’s moving at pace at that moment and a crowd comes in and knocks him down.

“There’s a question mark I guess around whether or not he would get onto that ball before [United keeper Senne] Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

“The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is tha Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. (It’s) certainly not clearly wrong.”

VAR John Brooks was of the same opinion as he said in the audio between him and referee Barrott: “Let’s roll it through firstly to see whether the attacker is going to get on the end of the ball.

“Just roll through real speed. So, at full speed, Isak maintains his momentum and likely gets on the end of it.

“OK, certainly not clearly wrong that he doesn’t. So I think the DOGSO confirmed.”

#837. How to become a football referee

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and said sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your plan and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

With a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

If you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:

In her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees new referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared."

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

As well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful."

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Sources: National Careers Service, GOV.UK, FA, IFA, SFA, and FAW.

#835. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

Ever wondered who makes sure your video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

Manchester United are in the market for a central defender and Mauricio Pochettino understands the need better than most

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#832. Aston Villa’s winless run continues with damaging Champions League defeat at Galatasaray

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa’s hopes of progressing to the Champions League knockout rounds were dented as they were beaten 1-0 at Galatasaray.

Unai Emery’s side won their first three games in the league phase but rather than bouncing back from a 3-0 defeat at Barcelona, they suffered another reverse in Istanbul.

Deniz Gul’s 77th minute header was the game’s first shot on target and was enough to seal all three points for the Turkish side.

With games against Paris St Germain and Borussia Dortmund to come either side of Christmas, Unai Emery’s men now have a challenge to finish in the top eight and earn a direct ticket into the knockout phase.

Even more worryingly, this latest loss made for six straight games without a win in all competitions, while Villa failed to register a single shot on target in the 90 minutes. their sixth consecutive defeat

The pre-match talk was about the state of the pitch at RAMS Park, with Galatasaray playing the weekend’s league match away from the stadium in order for the surface to undergo emergency repairs.

As a result, Villa were unable to train on it ahead of the game and the pitch was plied with sand.

But the visitors initially acquitted themselves well and managed the cauldron of noise as they enjoyed a controlled start, with their best moment coming when they made a quick break down the right and the ball ended up with Johan Manzambi, but he could not get a shot away.

Galatasaray came into it as the first half progressed, but did not test Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, who will have welcomed a quiet opening after his recent troubles.

The intensity increased at the start of the second half and there were two flashpoints as tempers flared.

First, John McGinn and Aleksey Batrakov went into the book after McGinn flew into his counterpart as revenge for a heavy challenge on Alysson by former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez.

There was another coming together as Joao Gomes was booked for stopping Yunus Akgun’s counter-attack.

The hosts suddenly had the bit between their teeth and they pushed Villa back, with Aleksey Batrakov flashing a volley well over, before a loose ball from a corner fell to Gul, who showed bravery to head the ball home while taking a kick in the face from Nicolas Jackson.

Arsenal wonderkid Ethan Nwaneri hasn't established himself on loan - and now faces further competition for his place

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ethan Nwaneri's Arsenal career appears to be floundering, with the on-loan Borussia Dortmund teenager facing a further transfer setback.

Nwaneri returns to his parent club tonight in the Champions League with the Bundesliga giants and is eligible to face Arsenal despite still being owned by the Gunners.

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

But after going out on loan at Marseille last term and heading to Dortmund this time, the teenager is yet to impress, with Arteta even admitting this week that “moments are not enough” for Nwaneri in his development and that consistency must follow.

A report from Sport Witness, likewise, reads as bad news for the 19-year-old, with the Gunners now pursuing a move for Gilberto Mora as soon as January.

Mora was the youngest player selected for the 2026 World Cup and has impressed hugely in his native Mexico, courting the attention of virtually every big club in Europe.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In attacking midfield areas, Arsenal already have the likes of Martin Odegaard, Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Max Dowman – with the latter two options on the wing – and should Arsenal bring in another teenage talent, Nwaneri's first-team opportunities would appear even scarcer.

FourFourTwo understands that the Gunners were open to offers for the starlet over the summer, opting to retain him and develop him at one of the best finishing schools in European football, though the paths of Nwaneri and Hale End colleague Myles Lewis-Skelly have been drastically different, thanks, in part, due to competition for places.

With Liverpool also circling for Mora, however, the Gunners may well have to present a particularly enticing package to secure the 18-year-old.

According to the report, the youngster has a release clause of around €25 million, making any move for him particularly costly – and suggesting that the Gunners could well incorporate him into their first team immediately.

Nwaneri, meanwhile, is valued by Transfermarkt at €25m. Arsenal return to Champions League action tonight against Dortmund at the Emirates Stadium.
