#830. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.

#829. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#828. Mauricio Pochettino admits Man United’s ‘situation is fragile’ but insists he has a ‘strong team’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mauricio Pochettino watched his Manchester United side lose 4-0 to Liverpool on Sunday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino has insisted he has taken over a "strong team" at Manchester United, despite acknowledging that their current predicament is a precarious one.

The Argentine's tenure as head coach began disastrously on Sunday with a heavy 4-0 defeat against rivals Liverpool, leaving them second bottom of the Premier League after 11 fixtures, ahead of only Crystal Palace.

Ahead of Wednesday's Champions League meeting in Lisbon, Sporting boss Paulo Fonseca dismissed the notion that United possess a fragility, and Pochettino pointed to their high-flying finish under Michael Carrick last term as evidence they can reverse their current slump.

"The situation is fragile," Pochettino said. "We are not fragile. We are a strong team, they showed that last season when they finished third and now we are playing in the Champions League.

"Sometimes things happen in football for different reasons. We need to identify why and already we are working on it. I think we are going to turn round the situation.

"We need to go game-by-game. In the end, being at Manchester United is about winning every single game, one is not more important than another.

"We are Manchester United and we need to believe we have the capacity to turn that situation. We are building our identity and that is the most important thing."

United captain Bruno Fernandes agreed that getting back to winning ways is his main focus and only then will the Portuguese midfielder restart talks over signing a new deal.

Fernandes, who joined United from Sporting in January 2020, is into the final year of his contract, which includes an option for another 12 months, although he has turned down two offers of an extension.

Asked what conditions have to be in place to sign a new long-term contract, Fernandes replied: “For us to start winning games and then we can start speaking about contracts. It’s not important now, it’s irrelevant.

“I know it’s my future and I shouldn’t look at it that way because I haven’t got much left in my contract but I’m more worried about getting results, trying to get the club into a position we can be proud of.

“We’ll have time to speak about that. We had conversations, the conversations stopped when that was not as important because the results and performances weren’t at the level they should have been.”

United have won two and lost two in this season’s Champions League, most recently coming from 2-0 behind at Old Trafford to claim a 3-2 win over Roma earlier this month.

Fernandes has played just one knockout tie – against Atletico Madrid in 2022 – during his stint at United.

He added: “When I started my career, I never had the opportunity in the first few years to play Champions League, so that was a faraway dream for me.

“I’m very proud of what I’ve achieved, even if I have only played one time, I still have got many years left in my career, I hope, so I’m going to have many opportunities to do that and why not this season?”

#827. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

#825. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#823. Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

Arsenal 1-1 Borussia Dortmund: The Gunners remain unbeaten in the Champions League but failed to capitalise at the Emirates

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal were held to a 1-1 draw in their Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund but remain on course to qualify in one of the automatic knockout spots.

The Gunners started the clash at the Emirates Stadium in quick fashion and controlled possession with short, slick passes and forward runs. Noni Madueke impressed on the right and set up Viktor Gyokeres to score the opening goal from outside the penalty area.

However, Mikel Arteta’s team slackened off in discipline as the half went on which allowed Dortmund to gain a foothold. The Bundesliga leaders then came out from half-time with renewed vigour and secured an equaliser through Maximilian Beier.

With the scores level both teams created further chances, Declan Rice hit the post and Jobe Bellingham had a goal disallowed, but neither could find the back of the net again.

The points were shared leaving Arsenal fifth in the league phase table with Dortmund one point below them in seventh.

Relive the updates from Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund, below:

Arsenal try their best to secure an equaliser but it’s not enough and the points are shared at the Emirates Stadium.

90 mins: Four minutes of added time to play.

87 mins: Merino has a history of scoring crucial goals in substitute appearances.

Time is against him here but Arsenal are pushing for the winner.

84 mins: Viktor Gyokeres receives a nice round of applause from the Arsenal fans as he departs the pitch.

Mikel Merino is on instead and will lead the line for the Gunners.

81 mins: The tempo has dropped again as the match enters the final 10 minutes.

Arsenal come forward in numbers but are propelled as Dortmund get every man behind the ball.

78 mins: Arsenal win a throw in high up the pitch and then are awarded a handball after it hits Marcel Sabitzer on the hand.

The resultant free kick could be a chance for the Gunners.

Martin Odegaard stands over it and curls a low cross into the box. He finds Hincapie over by the far post, the defender pulls the ball back and a deflection bounces the ball onto the post!

75 mins: 15 minutes to play at the Emirates Stadium and Arsenals reinforcements have brought a bit of control to the game.

The cross comes in from the right and Gyokeres dives for the ball.

He meets it with a strong header but misses the target!

70 mins: From a Dortmund attack to an Arsenal one after Rice threads the ball through to Eze on the left side of the pitch.

He rolls the ball onto his right foot and shoots but a deflection takes the ball wide of the far post and out for a corner.

The corner is defended by Dortmund and Arsenal must build another attack.

67 mins: Jobe Bellingham thinks he’s sent Dortmund ahead.

Ryerson takes a shot from the right side of the box and Kepa drops to make the save.

He palms the ball to Bellingham who turns it into the open goal but the offside flag goes up!

64 mins: Mikel Arteta makes a triple change.

Eberechi Eze, Bruno Guimares and Jurrien Timber are all introduced.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ben White and Christos Tzolis are the men replaced.

#821. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Yeremy Pino is the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow-card suspension

Crystal Palace's Yeremy Pino has become the latest Premier League player to receive a yellow card suspension after accumulating five bookings since the 2026-27 season began.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash were the first players to receive a ban for collecting five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 17 players sitting on four bookings after 11 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have received a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (five yellow cards)

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Chema Andres - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Yeremy Pino - Crytsal Palce (yellow card suspension)

#820. Why Arsenal’s crazy festive fixture run could hand them the Premier League title in record time

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?

Tom Hancock started freelancing for FourFourTwo in April 2019 and has also written for the Premier League and Opta Analyst, among others. He supports Wycombe Wanderers and has a soft spot for Wealdstone. A self-confessed statto, he has been known to watch football with a spreadsheet (or several) open...

#819. Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany

His life is a reflection of contemporary German history, addressed via his songs and sharp wit. At 90, he's as feisty as ever.

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

#818. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#816. Ukraine: Zelenskyy says security deal could go to referendum

The US has broached the idea of Kyiv giving up the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, the Ukrainian president said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of ‌Donbas ⁠in exchange ⁠for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.

The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.

The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would ⁠Ukraine ​withdraw from Donbas?'"

Zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a ‌strong ​and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question ​to the public in a referendum.

"That ​is why ⁠I believe NATO is back on the ⁠agenda. ​But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."

Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.

He also warned about Moscow's plan to  change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.

Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.

"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.

"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Friday, the EU said several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.

Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.

The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its ⁠forces ⁠had captured the ​settlement of Tersianka in ​Ukraine’s southeastern ​Zaporizhzhia ‌region, news agency Interfax reported.

Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian ​forces had struck Ukrainian energy and ​transport infrastructure used by ⁠the ​military, along with ammunition ​depots and ​drone production ‌and storage sites.

Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.

Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.

#815. Senegal confirmed AFCON 2025 champions after appeal

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled Senegal to be the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, which concluded in January; Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final but were stripped of the title in March, which led to their appeal

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has announced Senegal as the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON).

In response, the Royal Moroccan Football Federation said it was 'astonished' by the decision and 'affirms its intention to pursue all available legal procedures to appeal the decision'.

Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final in January but were stripped of the title by a Confederation of African Football (CAF) appeal board in March for breaking competition rules by walking off the pitch because of a late disallowed goal and a controversial penalty awarded to their opponents.

Senegal's protest caused a delay of over 15 minutes and when their players returned to the pitch, Morocco's Brahim Diaz missed the penalty to force the match into extra time, with Pape Gueye going on to score the winner.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025)," a CAS statement read.

"The decision rendered by the CAF appeal board is set aside and the decision by the CAF disciplinary board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal)."

Morocco's appeal was initially rejected but a CAF panel did uphold it and found Senegal's walk-off meant they had forfeited the match, awarding a 3-0 win to Morocco.

CAF said Senegal infringed on article 82 of AFCON's regulations, which states if a team refuses to play or leaves the ground before the end of regulation time without the referee's authorisation, it will be considered the loser and eliminated from the competition.

Article 84 states any team that violates article 82 will be permanently eliminated and lose the match 3-0.

However, the IFAB laws of the game state: "The decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play, including whether or not a goal is scored and the result of the match, are final."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Senegal appealed to CAS, calling the decision "a travesty", and have now been reinstated as champions.

The Moroccan federation wrote to the CAS earlier on Tuesday asking them to postpone the announcement of their decision. They wanted CAS to investigate allegations that one of the members of the CAS panel - Ulrich Haas - spoke on the telephone to the president of the Senegal FA Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.

CAS confirmed it had received a challenge petition 'a few minutes' before the announcement but decided 'there were insufficient grounds at this stage to postpone the notification of the award'.

In April, IFAB - who are football's law makers - introduced a law stating that any players who leave the field of play in protest at a referee's decision can be sent off. The adoption of this law is at the discretion of the competition organiser.

Sky Sports News' Chief Correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:

"Common sense has prevailed because the Court of Arbitration for Sport have effectively confirmed that Senegal did win the 2025 AFCON.

"Morocco were very unhappy because they felt that the rules of the tournament had been broken by Senegal when they left the pitch. They felt that at that stage Senegal should have forfeited the game.

"They went to the African Confederation Appeal Board and there was an appeal hearing in March. That appeal decided that yes, Morocco were right and they should be the winners and the result of the game was changed from a 1-0 win to Senegal to a 3-0 win to Morocco.

"Then we had the next chapter in this story because Senegal were also very unhappy with the decision of the appeal board, so they went to CAS in Switzerland. There was a hearing in October and now we have had the decision - a unanimous decision from the three judges.

"I don't want to tempt fate, because let's wait and see what the Moroccan Federation say, but what I would say to you is that they have fought this all the way, they believe that this is an injustice and they are one of the most powerful football associations in Africa.

"They are co-hosts of the next World Cup in 2030 and they have a very close relationships with the leadership at FIFA.

"I'm not suggesting that anything untoward is going on, but they still do have options. For instance, if they feel there has been something wrong in the procedures at the CAS hearing, they could go to the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

"I think the Moroccan Federation, according to what Reuters are reporting this afternoon, are unhappy with the way CAS handled this appeal and they have complained to CAS because they believe that one of the judges actually spoke on the phone to the president of the Senegal Federation on Sunday afternoon, so perhaps that is an avenue that they are going to explore."

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025).

The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal).

The FSF appealed to CAS against a decision of the CAF Appeal Board declaring that the Senegal national team forfeited the AFCON 2025 final and recording the Moroccan national team as the winners.

In their appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of the Referee, Mr Jean-Jacques Ngambo Ndala, to resume the match at the 109th minute (90+19) during the AFCON 2025 final and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.

The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the Referee's decision did not fall under the 'field of play' doctrine, as it cannot be applicable to the disciplinary consequences of the Senegalese team's behaviour. The FRMF alleged that, by leaving the pitch temporarily, the Senegalese team breached Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations, which should have led the Referee to bring the match to an early conclusion. The FRMF also argued that the Referee erred in law and that his decision was arbitrary.

After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority. By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.

In the Panel's view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee's decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee's decision was covered by the 'field of play' doctrine. Since Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations are intended solely to determine the outcome of a match when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently, they are therefore not applicable in this case. In conclusion, the Panel considers that in resuming the match, the Referee did not err in law.

The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as "arbitrary". On the contrary, the Referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.

Regarding the disciplinary aspects of the case, the Panel noted that the FSF, the FSF coach Mr. Pape Thiaw, and certain players had already been sanctioned by CAF following separate disciplinary proceedings.

Consequently, the appeal by the FSF was upheld. This was a unanimous decision by the CAS Panel.

#813. Author Correction: Reference genomes and fossils revise bat family phylogeny and biogeography

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The Original Article was published on 23 September 2026

Correction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11007-3 Published online 23 September 2026

In the version of the article initially published, in the Abstract, “Biogeography” section and Conclusion, the epoch in which bats originated was given as the “late Palaeocene” but should have been “late Cretaceous/early Palaeocene”. This has now been corrected in the HTML and PDF versions of this article.

#811. Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim

DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

This article was originally written in German.

#809. What Is Roaching? Unpacking the Dating Term That’s Bugging People Out

As dating evolves, so does the terminology. Take roaching, for example, which has crawled into the internet lexicon to refer to a person dating multiple people.

Dating is all about kissing a frog or two—and possibly a roach?

As the culture of dating continues to swipe its way forward, new terminology also crawls onto the scene, and the language doesn’t always create a beautiful mental image.

Take, for example, “roaching,” which refers to when one person is dating multiple people at once without telling the other individuals that they’re also talking to others.

"The name comes from the saying that if you see one cockroach, there are many more hiding,” dating coach Amy Chan told USA Today in an interview published Nov. 23. “In terms of dating, when you find out there’s one other person, that tends to mean there are several more."

And as the author of Unsingle: How to Date Smarter and Create Love That Lasts author explained, "This often happens in the early stages of dating, where commitment and labels aren’t clearly defined, so they justify that they’re not doing anything wrong."

The consciousness of someone’s actions also plays a part in roaching, like with “intentional roaching.”

"They intentionally conceal the fact that there are other people in the picture," Chan continued. "They’re lying by omitting information."

But when the truth comes out, the roach might not be able to survive the apocalyptic impact their actions had on the other person.

"This can be hard to bounce back from,” Chan said, “as they don’t know how long they’ve been left in the dark, and they feel like they cannot trust again."

Meanwhile, relationship coach Sabrina Bendory noted that unintentional roaching—where one person feels deceived despite the other’s lack of intended deception—could be a result of poor communication. As she posited to USA Today, "The real issue is that two people are assuming two different things."

In fact, Bendory, author of The Feminine Code: Deprogramming a Toxic & Narcissistic Dating Culture, cautioned daters to temper their anticipation in the beginning of a dating relationship.

As she put it, “You can't go into the early stages of a relationship, or in this case it would be a situationship, with any sort of expectations or assumptions.”

Of course, many celebs have been vocal about their preference to have multiple partners in their relationship—although unlike roaches, they’ve kept the conversation candid with all involved. Read on for stars who have tried non-monogamy.

The "Lonely" singer confirmed he has multiple wives in May 2025.

As for how many? He said, “I’ll just leave that to your imagination.”

And while the musician has multiple rules as part of his polyamorous setup—including a hierarchy structure and that his wives can't have other partners—he emphasized they're making it work.

“You got to be mature enough to know that if this is the situation that I'm going to park in, I have to communicate,” he said on the We Need to Talk podcast. “This I like, this I don't like. This I'm for, this I'm not for, and this is what I'm willing to deal with, and this is what I'm not willing to deal with. And once y'all lay down those rules, just abide by them. It's literally that simple.”

The Queer Eye star and their husband Mark Peacock go through "seasons" of non-monogamy.

"I'm all about a season," Jonathan said on The Mitch Churi Chat Show in February 2026, noting that while many might see open relationships as a Pandora’s Box that can’t be closed back up once opened, "We have been able to thread that needle."

However, an open communication about boundaries is paramount to making it work.

"We've been able to go kind of back and forth based off of what is going on in our lives," the hairstylist added, "and that works for us."

"Polyamorous is definitely not something I could do," the JVN Hair founder admitted. "I just don't have time to deal with a third person's needs. That's a lot."

For RuPaul and his husband Georges LeBar, having an open relationship works because "it's just realistic," the TV host explained to The New Yorker in 2024. "There’s no such thing as monogamy with men."And ultimately, it just made sense for the couple."We didn't decide," the RuPaul's Drag Race star, who met his husband at New York nightclub Limelight in 1994 some two decades before they wed, told Vanity Fair in 2019. "The hoax is that monogamy is actually something that can actually happen. I wouldn't want to put restraints on the person I love the most on this planet. I wouldn't do that to someone I love, my very best friend."And having an open marriage doesn't make them question their love for each other."Listen, if you get something happening that you cannot resist and that's going to make you happy, go for it," RuPaul continued. "Go for it. Because the truth is, I know in my heart of hearts like I've never known anything before, that man loves me more than anything else in this world."

Kody Brown once said, "Love should be multiplied, not divided."And for decades, he was in a plural marriage with wives Meri Brown, Janelle Brown, Christine Brown and Robyn Brown—their journey documented on the series Sister Wives."I just fell in love," the father of 18 said on the first episode in 2010, "and then I fell in love again and I fell in love again."However, he's since fallen out of love with polygamy. Christine and Kody announced their breakup in November 2021 and he and Janelle confirmed their separation in December 2022. A month later, Meri revealed their decision to "permanently terminate" their marriage. As a result, Robyn is Kody's sole wife."I'm not an advocate of plural marriage, but I've had my own experience in it and I've had my own failures in it," he told People in December 2023. "Because of that, I'm like, you got to be really, really wise about who is doing it, how they're doing it."And while Kody said it can work for some people, he noted "there's those marriages that have people who know each other very, very, very well, and they still don't work."Some of Kody's exes have since embraced monogamy—like Christine, who wed David Woolley in 2023 and has said on the show she "wouldn't live polygamy again." Others, like Janelle, have said they "would consider a plural marriage again."As for wife Robyn, she said on a 2024 episode she'd do plural marriage again if she could guarantee a "positive successful experience."

Willow Smith brought a discussion on non-monogamy to the red table."With polyamory, I feel like the main foundation is the freedom to be able to create a relationship style that works for you," Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's youngest said on a 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, "and not just stepping into monogamy because that's what everyone around you says is the right thing to do."And Jada and fellow cohost Adrienne Banfield-Norris listened to what Willow had to say. "The main reasons why monogamists' relationships or why marriage, why divorces happen is infidelity," the "Whip My Hair" artist continued. "Let's say you haven't always been the kind of person that wanted to have sex all the time, but your partner is. Are you gonna be the person to say, 'Just because I don't have these needs, you can't have them either?'"But that doesn't mean they always agreed. And when Willow's Gammy raised questions about sex, Willow replied, "In my friend group, I'm the only polyamorous person, and I have the least sex out of all my friends."

Shailene Woodley believes the only opinions that matter in a relationship are the ones of the people in it."Listen, I’m someone who has experienced both an open relationship and a deeply monogamous relationship in my life, and I think we’re in a day and age where there should be no rules except for the ones designed by two people in a partnership — or three people, whatever floats your boat!" the Big Little Lies star told The New York Times in 2020. "But there has to be a level of responsibility in any relationship dynamic, and that responsibility is simply honesty and communication and trust. Apart from that, it’s really none of our business what people choose to do with their lives."

When you’re mad at Ne-Yo about his polyamorous relationships, he doesn’t give it another thought."Them: 'NEYO WE DON'T APPROVE OF YOUR POLY RELATIONSHIP,'" the singer wrote on his Instagram Stories in February, later adding, “Fun fact: I don't care."And Ne-Yo—who was married to Crystal Renay for almost seven years before they finalized their divorce in 2023—introduced the internet to his four girlfriends in March 2025.

"It works," the Grammy winner said on a February 2025 episode of the Rickey Smiley Morning Show. "Everybody’s honest. Everybody’s telling the truth. Everybody is consenting. I feel like I wasted a lot of time just being dishonest about things to the point where had I taken this approach initially I probably could have saved myself a lot of headache and heartache."However, that doesn't mean polyamory works for everybody."Please understand that I'm not in here saying that everybody should try what I'm trying and do what I'm doing," Ne-Yo clarified. "I'm telling y'all what works for me. I'm showing y'all what works for me. And if you agree, cool. If you don't, cool. Either way you slice it, I'm happier than I've ever been, I'm more zen than I've ever been and that's what it is—that's the important part. I don't need everybody to agree. I'm not doing it for y'all."

While Bella Thorne has been in a relationship solely with fiancé Mark Emms since 2022, she'd previously been in non-monogamous relationships."It’s a really fun experience and I have been able to capture that a couple times, and I just love that idea,” the Disney Channel alum told Cosmopolitan in 2019. "I love loving two people at once. I love sharing stories with three people in one room. So, I’m always trying to find ways to make it work because I think it really would make me happy."However, she understood it wasn’t the right fit for everyone.“A lot of my partners start out like 'what?’ and I’m like, 'Bro, this is who I am,’” Bella added at the time. "So, you’re either down or you're not down and I totally understand if you’re not down. At this point in my life, I want to find what makes me the happiest, and that is the mission I am on. If you don’t want to be on that mission with me, then okay, I totally understand. If it will hurt you too much, then we’re not right for each other at this moment in my life because this is what I’m looking for.”

As for Yungblud, he's shared he identifies as pansexual and polyamorous.

"I probably would say now, I am polyamorous," the musician, also known as Dominic Harrison, told Attitude in 2020. "Before I didn’t f--king know what I was. I was meeting people and learning… by meeting them and talking about sexuality and gender, I [was] going, 'Oh my f--king God, maybe I’m this, if I’m going to be f--king close to anything on the spectrum.'"

Bob the Drag Queen has two partners and is happy they’re in other relationships too."I have a partner in L.A. and a partner in Georgia," The Traitors star said on an April 2025 episode of Boyfriend Material With Harry Jowsey. “They know each other. They’re not super close, but they do like each other. My partners also have partners too, which is great for me. I’m a really independent person, and I actually don’t like the idea of being someone's everything. I actually kind of get exhausted at the idea of being around someone all the time. So having your partner have a partner is really a gift."

In 2018, Nico Tortorella and Bethany C. Meyers tied the knot and penned an essay about their relationship."If you had to label it, Nico and I are in a queer polyamorous relationship," the I Am More Than My Body author wrote in a piece for Them. "Labels that help people understand, but not labels that define us. Most think we planned this and one day decided we would be multiple-love kind of people. We didn’t. It’s just the way our relationship developed over 12 years."However, Nico and Bethany's relationship shifted to monogamous during the coronavirus pandemic and as they welcomed kids Kilmer and Pesce Pearl."To answer your question point blank: Are you still open?" the Younger star noted on a 2024 episode of their podcast Full of Shift. "No. Right now, we're not." However, they're, uh, open to the possibility of re-exploring non-monogamy again one day."Is that to say that in the future it could be different?" Nico continued. "Who knows?"

From Omarion’s perspective, monogamy just doesn’t hit the right note.And as the singer explained on a February 2025 episode of Sherri, "being open is important" to him."The women just truly outnumber the men," he told host Sherri Shepherd, later adding, "It’s only a few good men. Whether or not it’s a physical thing, we end up fostering the next generation as well….Why not have our queens align with that? It takes a village. It’s not gonna just be one man. You can get married—that man still aint going to be just your man. He’s gonna be there for his daughter, he’s going to be there for his mom, his grandmother.”So as Omarion sees it, “This concept isn’t really foreign, it’s just a little old and it’s meant to be upgraded.” And he’d like there to be more discussions on the topic."I love this conversation because I think when men are open and honest that they don’t wanna have just this one thing for the rest of their life, it gives a woman the opportunity to choose and further understand a man," the musician added. "Because I think that women don’t really understand a man. Certain women do, but there’s a larger conversation that has to be had about understanding men and how we’re meant to spread our seed."
