“I don't remember a lot,” she explained on Fit for TV: The Reality of The Biggest Loser. “I remember hearing the helicopter. I just felt like I was floating. And then my grandpa was there. And then I saw darkness. But then I saw light. So I knew, I knew I died that day.”

“My organs were literally shutting down,” she continued. “I didn't realize that I had rhabdomyolysis. And rhabdomyolysis is your body's way of saying, ‘I'm going to shut down on you.’”

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

#771. Dancing With the Stars' Derek Hough Details Childhood Abuse

DWTS host Derek Hough shared a traumatic part of his upbringing with sister Julianne Hough in which he experienced abuse at 12 years old while living in Utah.

As the Dancing With the Stars judge looked back on the beginning of his path to becoming a professional dancer, he shared one of the darker chapters of his childhood with sister Julianne Hough while being raised in the suburbs of Salt Lake City, Utah.

"The neighborhood that we grew up in, we definitely just had some neighbors that weren't great. They pretty much terrorized my family in a lot of ways," Derek shared in his Nov. 23 documentary Symphony of Dance per USA Today, stating, "One of my neighbors was, for lack of a better word, just really inappropriate with me physically."

In addition, the 41-year-old explained of the traumatic period, "They hung me up in a tree by my ankles, put a gun to my head, spat on me, hogtied me up in a field and left me there."

As such, enduring the abuse led to "a lot of emotion" for the then-12-year-old, who was raised alongside his DWTS costar as well as their older siblings Sharee, 49, Marabeth, 45 and Katherine, 44, by parents Bruce Hough and Mariann Heaton in the Mormon community. Julianne has previously shared that a painful part of her upbringing came at the hands of a neighbor in their cul-de-sac who she said sexually abused her at age 4.

"I just didn't understand where I was going," Derek said in the Hulu project about his reaction to the harmful treatment. "I was kind of left to my own devices."

And at first, the trauma pushed the choreographer further away from his future as a ballroom pro.

As he detailed, "I was a 12-year-old. I would skip school. I would skip dance. I wouldn't go. My dad was at work, and my mom was off, and [I was] just floating around with no direction."

Fortunately, Derek was "relieved" when he met mentors Corky Ballas and Shirley Ballas—parents of DWTS coach Mark Ballas—who soon moved Derek, and eventually Julianne, to London to attend drama academy Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

"Moving away was great because I was getting away from something," he said. "I was leaving this wounded boy, and I was gonna go become this success. I was gonna go work hard and achieve things and overcome things."

And the Emmy winner did exactly that, noting how the professional performers in his new world made him realize at the time, "This is what I want to do. I want to be like these guys."

Julianne alluded to her siblings undergoing hardship similar to her own on The Jamie Kern Lima Show Aug. 15 while telling her story, noting, "By the way, I'm not the only one in my family that had gone through similar things, so that was a very challenging thing to come to terms with."

Read on for a closer look at the Hough family tree.

The Hough family patriarch is originally from Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, and met future wife Mariann Heaton on the ballroom team at Ricks College (now Brigham Young University-Idaho).

Bruce and Mariann—both from Mormon families and the children of ballroom-dancing parents—settled in Salt Lake City. There he worked as a communications executive and co-founded supplement maker Nutraceutical Corporation, which, according to Deseret News, reached a valuation of $300 million under his watch before it was sold in 2017.

Bruce also ventured into politics, serving two terms as state Republican Party chair and running for congress in 2023.

While he didn't win that race, he told Deseret News at the time that he was running for his family's future. "I’ve got 10 kids, I’ve got 22 grandkids and growing," he explained. "And I really feel that America’s promise is in jeopardy for those grandkids especially."

Of his most famous offspring, he quipped, "I never thought that those dance lessons would pay off,” noting that he took the most pride in hearing from others that son Derek Hough and daughter Julianne Hough were some of the "kindest people…in the entertainment business.”

In addition to Derek and Julianne, Bruce shares daughters Sharee Hough Selman, Marabeth Poole and Katherine Hough with Mariann. After they divorced in the late 1990s, he married Debra Francom Hough, also a parent of five.

Mariann grew up in Idaho Falls with three brothers.

She and Bruce were in the process of divorcing when Julianne and Derek, then 10 and 13, moved to London to attend the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

Their leaving was "devastating," Mariann recalled on a 2019 episode of The Minds Gym podcast. But they wanted to dance and, she explained, "The biggest thing that kept me going is that I grew up feeling very dominated over and controlled. Love my parents, but that was like a generational thing."

However, she added, "I'm grateful for that now because…it made me sway to I love having free agency." It was also "so important" for her to pass that on to her kids, she said, and "all of them are so not afraid to go travel and do all these things."

Mariann, now based in Franklin, Tenn., is a painter and has credited husband Aaron Nelson for supporting and encouraging her work as an artist.

Sharee married husband Mark Selman when she was 19 and they share six kids.

The eldest of Bruce and Mariann's brood danced at Ballet West in Utah and these days runs her own fitness business, Hough Werks, teaching yoga and dance.

Her "dynamic" firstborn "just came into this world with a lot of energy," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. Sharee's "little mind was just going all the time, just super creative" and "self-motivated."

Moreover, with 11 years between Sharee and her youngest sister, "Julianne thinks she has two moms."

Marabeth is "just a beautiful spirit" who "loves her own space," Mariann said of her second child, and she "puts on these little retreats in Nashville for women."

She left Utah for Music City to "be a country star," baby sister Julianne shared on the Not Skinny but Not Fat podcast in September 2025, and now makes the most of her positive energy as a realtor and holistic health coach, as well as a singer-songwriter.

Marabeth married Michael Poole in 2002 and they live in Nashville with son Aidan.

Daughter Katherine, a mother of three, "just makes you smile," Mariann said on The Minds Gym, "and she's just real."

The esthetician was in a relationship with Tony Schnur before his death from brain cancer in 2023. "It’s unfair that I found my soulmate, my best friend, my partner in life, only to lose you too soon," Katherine posted on Instragram in February 2025, marking the second anniversary of his passing. "I miss you every day."

But Katherine has persevered, Julianne gushing on Not Skinny But Not Fat, "She has three beautiful daughters and she has all these activities and she plans all these things, and I'm in awe of her."

And on Sept. 24, 2025, Katherine shared that she had found love again, writing on Instagram alongside a montage of sweet photos, "After walking through so much loss and heartache, I never imagined I’d find this kind of love again. Chris is the man I prayed for, kind, generous, loving, patient, and such a gift not only to me but to my girls."

Born May 17, 1985, Derek joined Dancing With the Stars as a pro in 2007. He won the Mirrorball Trophy a record six times and is a four-time Emmy winner for choreography.

After his last competitive turn around the floor in 2016, Derek returned to DWTS as a fulltime judge in 2020.

He met fellow dancer Hayley Erbert in 2015 and, after navigating some "insane obstacles," as he put it on Couple Things With Shawn Johnson and Andrew East, they got married in August 2023.

As a couple they powered through Hayley's life-threatening health scare, a brain hemorrhage that required emergency surgery just four months after their wedding, and in July 2025 they announced they were expecting their first child together.

Posting a photo of dad Bruce dancing at his and Hayley's wedding, Derek wrote on Facebook in April 2024, "Smart, kind and thoughtful. I hope to be as good as a father as he has been to his family."

The baby of the Hough family was born July 20,1988. She joined DWTS in 2007 along with Derek and proceeded to win her first two seasons on the show.

She left in 2009 to pursue acting and scored a breakthrough role in 2010's Burlesque (though her big-screen debut was actually playing an unnamed Hogwarts student in 2001's Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) before scoring the lead in the 2011 Footloose remake. Julianne returned to the ballroom as a judge from 2014 to 2017, winning an Emmy for choreography along the way, and has cohosted DWTS with Alfonso Ribeiro since 2023.

Julianne married Brooks Laich in 2017 but they split up in 2020, eventually finalizing their divorce in 2022.

She said on The Jamie Kern Lima Show in 2024 that going through a divorce gave her a chance to "reconnect" with her mom and dad, and they "showed up" for her.

"I needed that," Julianne explained. "I reclaimed my parental relationship with them and I got to be the kid and they got to take care of me. And that was the most healing [thing]."

Reflecting on her and Derek becoming the stars of the family, Julianne said on Not Skinny But Not Fat that there was "no jealousy" between their other siblings, "but there is a sadness that maybe there wasn't an opportunity for them to experience it."

Sharee, Marabeth and Katherine are "so, so, so happy," Julianne continued. "They have great lives, and they love their life. But we had an opportunity that they didn't have, and it's hard.”

And while she and Derek have a special connection, "they were super close as sisters growing up,” Julianne said. “So, I didn't get to have the closeness of sisters and that bond. [And] they have marriages and kids and I don't have that experience."

Meanwhile, all five siblings "get along really well," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. "I think the hard part is being away from each other, because there is some kind of a synergy when they all get together."

#769. Menopause can speed up brain ageing — hormone therapy might protect it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Fieldhouse is a reporter for Nature in Sydney, Australia.

Hormonal changes during menopause could explain why Alzheimer’s disease affects more women than men. Credit: Maskot/Getty

Certain types of hormone therapy for menopause are linked to better memory performance and a reduced risk of mild cognitive impairment, according to data presented at a neuroscience conference that began on 14 November. The findings suggest that certain therapies could be protective against the brain changes that often precede Alzheimer’s disease, say the authors, although more research is needed to confirm this effect.

The research is part of a series of studies presented at the Society for Neuroscience’s Neuroscience 2026 conference that reveal differences in cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression on the basis of biological sex or life stage.

Women are twice as likely to develop AD than are men. But the reasons for these sex differences are poorly understood and poorly studied, say researchers in the field. “The women’s health gap is huge,” Liisa Galea, a neuroscientist at the University of Toronto in Canada, told reporters at the conference, which was held in Washington DC. Part of the problem is that studies often do not analyse sex differences, adds Galea.

Researchers think that hormonal changes that happen during menopause could partially explain why the disease affects women and men differently. For instance, going through menopause early, between 40 and 45 years old, is thought to increase a woman’s risk of cognitive decline and developing AD. Some studies have found that oestrogen — which decreases during menopause — has a protective effect on the brain.

Mateja Perović, a neuroscientist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, and her team wanted to know whether menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), which is used to supplement oestrogen levels and treat symptoms of menopause, can slow cognitive ageing and reduce the risk of developing AD. Perović says previous studies have showed mixed results, but these studies had not differentiated between the different types of MHT1.

The team analysed the cognitive function of around 14,000 women who received different types of MHT or none at all2. They also compared cognitive function of women using MHT who had a genetic risk of developing AD with those who didn’t.

They found that oestradiol-based treatments — which contain a compound that is chemically identical to the oestrogen produced by the body — were associated with better episodic memory in women without cognitive impairment than were treatments containing a mix of natural and synthetic oestrogens. Episodic memory refers to the ability to learn and recall information. A deficit in this can be an early symptom of AD. Women who did not receive any MHT also showed better episodic memory than those who received the mixed-oestrogen treatments.

Oestradiol-based MHT also showed benefits for women who were not genetically predisposed to AD and had mild cognitive impairment, whereas the mixed-oestrogen MHT did not.

Both treatment types were beneficial for other types of long-term memory function compared with no MHT for women who had mild cognitive impairment and carried a gene called APOE4, which is linked to an increased risk of AD. But MHT use did not affect the risk of progressing to dementia, suggesting that the treatments might improve a person’s cognitive function without preventing the disease.

When the researchers looked at structural brain changes using imaging techniques, they found that women with the APOE4 gene who took oestradiol had higher cortical thickness and less white-matter damage than did women not receiving MHT. Decreased cortical thickness, caused by the loss of neurons, is associated with decreased brain function and can be an early indicator of cognitive impairment. The findings suggest that oestradiol-based MHT might be particularly beneficial for women at higher risk of developing AD, says Perović.

Mia Schaumberg, who studies healthy brain ageing at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Sippy Downs, Australia, says it is promising that research is considering individual risk factors, such as genetics, and differences in MHT composition when looking at women’s cognitive health. “It is starting to gain the attention that it deserves,” she adds.

Although Susan Davis, an endocrinologist and researcher at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, says the effect of MHT on AD risk needs to be investigated in a randomized clinical trial to validate the findings of this study.

#768. Watford set to appoint former Romania boss Iordanescu

Edward Iordanescu's most recent job was with Legia Warsaw, who he left in October 2025

Watford are set to appoint Edward Iordanescu as their new manager.

BBC Three Counties Radio report the Romanian is due to become the Hornets' sixth manager inside 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United in his 18th game in charge.

The 48-year-old is understood to be arriving in the UK on Tuesday to sign his contract and plans to bring three members of staff with him and hopes to be in the dugout for Wednesday's Championship fixture at home to Blackburn Rovers (19:45 GMT).

Iordanescu guided Romania at Euro 2024 where they topped their group ahead of Belgium with all four sides ending level on four points from three games before a 3-0 defeat against the Netherlands in the Round of 16.

Iordanescu - whose father Anghel had three spells in charge of the Romanian national team, leading them in two World Cups and two European Championships - left his last role at Polish club Legia Warsaw in October 2025.

It was the 48-year-old's ninth club over a 15-year coaching career which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj among others in his homeland.

Dionisi, who departed with the Hornets in 21st, four points above the relegation zone, was only appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

The 46-year-old Italian was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

#767. Tom Brady Admits to Parenting “Mistakes” Raising His 3 Teenage Kids

Tom Brady likened being a parent to his teenage kids Jack, Benjamin and Vivian to his experience as a quarterback, admitting that, despite his seven Super Bowl wins, “I threw a lot of interceptions.”

Tom Brady knows that all parents drop the ball sometimes.

Since becoming dad to son Jack, 19, with ex-girlfriend Bridget Moynahan, as well as son Benjamin, 16, and daughter Vivian, 13, with ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, the seven-time Super Bowl champ admitted there are some losses among his many wins as a parent.

“Well, I’ve made a lot of mistakes,” Brady said on the Nov. 22 episode of the High Performance podcast. “So, a lot like quarterback. I threw a lot of interceptions. And with every one I’ve tried to learn.”

And with that effort, the 49-year-old added, “I hope I’m a better parent today than I was when I first started having kids. And hopefully I’m a better parent 10 years from now.”

So, what is Brady’s game plan for becoming the best dad he can be?

“The important thing for me in my personal life is to go where my kids are at, too,” he explained. “Not to say, ‘Hey kids, pay attention to the things I'm doing or what's important to me.’ It’s been a really important lesson for me over the years to go to my kids and say, ‘What’s really important to you? What’s driving you? Or what are you scared of, or how can I pay attention to the things that you value?’”

Finding ways to connect with his kids is a skill Brady said he developed from leading football teams during his 23 seasons as an NFL quarterback.

“Part of that is just being really open and present and also trying to be really relatable to the younger [generation],” he continued, “which I was very fortunate to learn over the course of my playing career.”

And now, Brady emphasized that he is simply trying to be “really present” and “non-judgmental” with his kids while imparting the wisdom he’s scored through his “years of experience.”

As he put it, he is “just trying to understand their perspective, but also trying to get them to understand my perspective a little bit, too.”

For a closer look at the special team Brady has built with his kids, keep reading…

#766. Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?

Janelt scores stunner as Brentford beat 10-man Everton

It had been some run for Everton captain James Tarkowski.

Prior to Monday night, the defender had received 74 yellow cards in the Premier League but had never been sent off - a top-flight record.

But that run came to an end at Brentford as he was given his first red card in his 351st Premier League appearance, although the decision has attracted plenty of debate.

His dismissal crucially means he will miss Sunday's Merseyside derby against Liverpool and also ruined David Moyes' record-breaking night as he took charge of his 593rd game as Everton boss - more than anyone else in the club's history.

The 4-0 loss was also the heaviest defeat Everton have had since Moyes returned to the club at the start of last year.

Tarkowski's dismissal proved a big talking point during and after the match, with opinions split on whether he should have gone. Even Moyes wasn't sure.

He told BBC Match of the Day: "My thoughts at the time, I didn't think it was but when I've looked at it again I think his foot is high. Is there enough force for it to be a red card? Not sure about that."

James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card

Just 15 minutes after Keane Lewis-Potter scored his second deflected strike of the evening, Everton skipper Tarkowski thundered into a challenge on Brentford's Yehor Yarmoliuk.

He won the ball but also followed through with the challenge forcefully. Initially, referee Craig Pawson deemed a foul and a yellow card was enough.

But, after an intervention from the video assistant referee (VAR) and studying the replay, Pawson changed the yellow for a red.

The Premier League match centre said on X: "After VAR review, the referee overturned the original decision of yellow card for Tarkowski for the challenge on Yarmoliuk and issued a red card for serious foul play.

"VAR: 'Point of contact is on the shin. He's got speed and intensity. Studs are high.'

"REF: 'After review, Everton No.6 commits a challenge that endangers his opponent's safety, making contact with the studs onto the shin. Cancelling the yellow card - and a red card.'"

Brentford 4-0 Everton: David Moyes post-match interview

Referees are asked to take into account several considerations for what counts as serious foul play including the speed of the challenge, its intensity, force and what degree of control there was.

But, as always, there was plenty of debate about whether it was the correct decision.

BBC Sport's football issues correspondent Dale Johnson, said: "Really not sure about this as a VAR red card.

"Yes, Tarkowski absolutely ticks the boxes for speed and intensity and leading high with studs showing.

"But the question marks are that Tarkowski made only small contact and didn't have a straight leg when he did so.

"Maybe his reputation played a part? Remember, he wrongly escaped a VAR red card against Liverpool for a challenge, which was along the same lines. He won the ball and then followed through into Alexis Mac Allister. Though that was a far stronger challenge."

BBC Radio 5 Live's - and former Blackburn Rovers striker - Chris Sutton, said on X: "Come on that's not a redâ¦ the game's gone."

Former Arsenal striker Alan Smith agreed the decision was harsh. He told Sky Sports: "Ten years ago we wouldn't have looked at it once and now we still [frame] it on the follow-through. I just can't see it.

"Only Tarkowski knows if he wanted to leave it high or if it was natural. The follow-through was just natural momentum.

"There's a bit of anger in there from Tarkowski and it's a little high but only he knows if he wanted to leave a little more on Yarmoliuk there."

Opinion was far from unanimous though, with both pundits in the Sky Sports studio adamant it was a clear red.

Former Liverpool centre-back Jamie Carragher said: "It's a red card. Tarkowski has got previous for tackles like that. He is a 90s defender, he tackles like that.

"He follows through with such force, it is excessive. You want to give him the benefit of the doubt but it's a red card."

He added: "You could argue was it a big enough mistake for VAR to get involved but I think we are splitting hairs. He doesn't need to do this."

While ex-Tottenham defender Toby Alderweireld added: "It's a red card, he knows what he is doing. 100%."

Everton fan calls Tarkoswki red card 'harsh'

Josh, Sheffield: Never a red for Tarkowski and I'm a Liverpool fan. What's he meant to do? Stop momentum. It's a good tackle and the player runs into the natural follow through

Robin, Essex: Another game ruined by VAR! Not straight leg tackle you can surely see he turned his foot around. Poor!

Rob, Manchester: These sorts of VAR decisions are making me turn off football. Why pay all that money to watch arbitrary decisions impact the game?

Lee: It is a sad day when a good tackle gets a player sent off. You slow anything down and dissect it you can find wrongs. Yellow was a bit much and the red ridiculous, we need ex players in the VAR decisions too.

Max, Oldham: What a load of nonsense the red card is. Tarkowski can't stop his momentum. VAR has ruined another game, plus what is the ref doing? He had a chance to stick with the yellow card. Another case of an official who has never played the game.

Paul, St Asaph: Tarkowski has got away with that same foul a few times. Do think he's the type of player to leave one in on purpose.

Anon: Yes it's a red - Tarkowski knows what he's doing, it's frustration and wanting to leave a bit on the player.

Chris, Chelmsford: He does it all the time at the borderline but about time he got one.

Woody, London: Lack of refinement masked as passion, classic Tarkowski tackle thereâ¦ glad to see him off.

George, Birmingham: Studs up in a tackle, he has to go. A clear red card for me.

#765. England, Northern Ireland, Scotland & Wales to host 2035 Women's World Cup

Spain beat England 1-0 to win the 2023 World Cup

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed.

It will be the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966.

The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament, and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters.

The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid included a proposal to use 19 venues, with 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales.

Monday's special meeting of Fifa's Congress also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams.

The news comes on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

Hosting World Cup means decade of excitement - Weir

Fifa announces UK will host 2035 Women's World Cup

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned.

But England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won.

England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play.

"Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations."

The English stadiums included in the 2035 bid are: Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford.

If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, it would still be considered in its current form.

Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium are the two Welsh venues, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland.

Northern Ireland missed out on co-hosting the men's Euros in 2028 after the UK government said in 2024 it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in time - but a redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in 2035.

A further three stadiums could be added - Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground, and a potential new Chelsea ground - which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa is yet to decide whether all four co-hosts will qualify automatically.

The Principality Stadium in Cardiff is one of two Welsh venues, along with the Cardiff City Stadium

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

"In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."

Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

IFA 'positive' over upgrades needed for World Cup

#763. 115 days, 39 private-jet flights, one election - Infantino's globetrotting

The private jets are operated by Qatar Executive - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors

Fifa president Gianni Infantino's globetrotting by private jet since his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup can be revealed.

BBC Sport found Infantino has taken 39 private flights - the equivalent of one every three days - and visited 32 different countries since the news emerged on 28 July.

Our research found he travelled more than 102,800 air miles and spent just under nine days in the air in the space of 115 days.

Critics have accused of Infantino of using tools only at his disposal as president to aid his campaign for re-election next March.

They questioned whether his re-election campaign may have partly motivated any promises made or support offered during those visits.

Fifa said Infantino had a "statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations".

However, he visited nearly double the 18 countries he did in the same period in 2025.

The initial Times story that revealed Infantino's World Cup plan led to a wave of criticism around the world.

But, as BBC Sport revealed, many observers feel Infantino is now the favourite to be re-elected in the spring after his rivals struggled to find a candidate to run against him until the last moment.

And it appears Infantino has managed to shore up support around the world, with critics suggesting his globetrotting was a key part of that strategy.

There has also been concern about the environmental impact of his extensive travels.

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - said Infantino's travelling was "part of his campaign".

He told BBC Sport: "The issue here is that Fifa does not have rules on campaign funding, so the president can claim that he's going there on official business when indirectly he's using that to campaign.

"And anyone else running against him very likely will not have the financial means to compete with that."

Infantino's position seemed vulnerable after it emerged he had been devising a plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, in a proposal called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Before FFE was abandoned, Infantino wrote to all 211 member associations saying they would receive $40m (Â£30m) if they backed the plan.

Lars-Christer Olsson - a former chief executive of Uefa - told BBC Sport the "important" question was "what does he promise and what are the conditions, as he already did when he promised cash if the members supported his FFE project?"

BBC Sport gleaned the information about where Infantino had been travelling to, and when, from postings on his social media accounts.

The reasons for his travels include holding meetings with football association presidents, opening pitches, meeting politicians and attending confederation gatherings.

The private jets he used are operated by Qatar Executive (QE) - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.

BBC Sport used flight-tracking records and the jet registrations of the Qatar Executive fleet to compile a detailed log of Infantino's flights, totalling at least 39 since the start of August. Fifa did not dispute the figure.

It said "all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations" and there are "rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official".

But Fifa declined to comment on how the use of QE flights impacts on the money available from the Qatar Airways sponsorship for the benefit of global football.

The governing body also declined to comment when asked when Infantino had last taken a commercial flight.

Olsson said: "What do these trips cost and who is paying, which are the implications for the total football community?

"Is he provided with transport in his private campaign with the idea of getting something back in return if he is elected? If Fifa is paying for private jets, would it not be better to invest this money in the member associations?"

Maduro said: "That's again a confusion between his role as president of Fifa and his role as candidate to Fifa presidency."

He said there were no regulations within Fifa on the "use of public money to support their campaign".

"There's no independent authority that controls that, there is no regulation of campaign funding," he said.

Infantino's trips included attending the Caribbean Football Union presidents' meeting and a junior football tournament in the Dominican Republic three weeks after FFE failed.

He then flew to Paris, where he attended the esports World Cup , alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.

On his Instagram account, Infantino said he had "pledged Fifa's support" for the Pakistan Football Federation president's development plans when he met him in the US in September.

A few days later, he referenced a "wonderful discussion" with the president of the Latvian Football Federation during a visit to Riga, describing him as "my dear friend".

During a visit to Indonesia in October for the final of the Fifa ASEAN Cup, he met presidents from the football federations of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Qatar, Singapore, Thailand and Timor-Leste.

He said: "Having your support and shared passion on this momentous occasion means a great deal and together we will continue driving this game forward."

And during a recent trip to Manila, he performed on stage as part of a quartet called the 'Backache Boys', alongside officials from the Asian Football Confederation, and the football federations of Malaysia and the Philippines.

Gianni Infantino opened a mini-pitch in Anguilla in November

Gianni Infantino visited the Philippines for the ASEAN Football Federation Ordinary Congress

Gianni Infantino in Qatar to oversee preparations for the Fifa U17 World Cup

Based on our log of Infantino's private-jet flights, we calculated he spent 213 hours and 49 minutes in the air, travelling about 102,870 air miles.

For the type of private jet Infantino was using, this would produce an estimated 1,673 tonnes of CO2e emissions.

That's equivalent to the emissions 252 people would accumulate on average in an entire year, according to European Union data, external. These figures are conservative estimates based on average fuel burn rates.

Fifa has also been criticised for expanding the number of teams at World Cups, and hosting them in multiple countries, thereby increasing the amount of travel. The 2026 World Cup was described as the 'most polluting World Cup ever'.

Freddie Daley, from the Cool Down Sport for Climate Action Network, said Infantino's behaviour was "emblematic of Fifa's approach to environmental sustainability under his leadership: total and utter disregard".

"Despite numerous pledges, Fifa has failed to deliver any significant plan on how it will achieve them and has instead gone backwards," he added.

Maduro said Fifa's support for initiatives on climate action - which included being a signatory of the United Nation's Sports for Climate Action Framework - was "window dressing".

Fifa did not directly respond to a question about its justification for the environmental impact caused by Infantino's extensive travelling.

A spokesperson for Fifa said its objectives were to "improve football constantly and promote it globally".

They added: "The Fifa president has a statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations.

"To do that, he travels around the world and attends Fifa's tournaments and events. Mr Infantino is elected until 18 March 2027, when the next Fifa presidential election will take place.

"Fifa has put in place rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official.

"The Fifa president routinely travels around the world for various duties, together with relevant officials, on business and tournament-related matters and strives to visit member associations of Fifa whenever he can.

"Fifa expenses are published in our annual report, and all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations.

"Fifa's money belongs to the 211 member associations and an increased investment to $6.35bn for the upcoming cycle reinforces our unwavering commitment to further supporting football development and access globally."

#762. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Konstantinos Tzolakis (Hull City): If you watched the Brighton game and wondered how on earth Hull won it was because Konstantinos Tzolakis was in goal. An unbelievable performance with five or six top-class saves. Big moments, big personality, he has stepped up every time. He's been one of the players of the season - I know it's a bit too early to crown people but if it stopped now he has to be goalkeeper of the season.

Janelt scores stunner and Lewis-Potter nets twice as Brentford beat 10-man Everton

James Hill (Bournemouth): He backed up getting into the England squad. Sometimes when people get called up they start to get above their stations but he didn't do that at all. He was in a really good state of form. A cheeky assist as well but defensively solid. He has been in my team a few times now - a centre-half who does his job without complaining.

Malick Thiaw (Newcastle): He divides opinion but he played really well and got his goal.

Keane Lewis-Potter (Brentford): Two goals against Everton and that was before the sending-off of James Tarkowski. Performed well again. Sneaky bargain buy of the century to be honest.

Teenager Williams-Barnett shines as Spurs beat Ipswich

Noah Okafor (Leeds): Two goals again. Leeds battered Chelsea and made them look unbelievably average. Nobody has been talking about how sneaky good Leeds have been, some really big performances this season.

Jack Rudoni (Coventry): Two assists in a must-win game against Crystal Palace. He stepped up big, fair play to him.

Elliot Anderson (Manchester City): The only person who actually showed a pulse in this game. He got a goal and showed pace and showed he wanted to be there. He tried his best to win a game of football.

Luca Williams-Barnett (Tottenham): Young man, a with goal and an assist. He just gave Spurs a spark we haven't seen for probably six or seven years now. He gave them that spark instantly and fair play to De Zerbi for putting him in. All the money spent, who knew it would be a home-grown talent in their youth team who would step up and really get the Spurs fans excited.

Ngumoha stars as Liverpool thrash 10-man Man Utd

Florian Wirtz (Liverpool): Unbelievable performance. He has had a bit of a purple patch since Jurgen Klopp has taken over Germany. Did really well in terms of finding the gaps, drifting between players and finding through balls and now adding goals. Now we are seeing the player we saw in Germany and I am buzzing for him.

Oli McBurnie (Hull City): The man of the moment. He works really hard, he does everything for the team to make sure they are there. He is solid defensively but then he gets two shots and two goals. Top performance from him.

Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool): He made Diogo Dalot look like he'd never played a game before, not the fact he has played over 250 games for Manchester United and has gone to World Cups with Portugal and made him look childish, Ran him every time and twisted him inside out and got his goal.

McBurnie stoppage-time double earns Hull win over 10-man Brighton

Frank Lampard (Coventry): In the biggest game of the season so far for him he made sure he got the job done. Big win. No new-manager bounce for Palace as Lampard gets the job done and he made some big calls.

#761. Christopher Lloyd, 88, Gives Look at Romance With Wife Lisa Lloyd, 56

Christopher Lloyd, 88, shared a sweet tribute to his wife Lisa Lloyd, 56, in honor of the couple's 10th anniversary. The two married in 2016 after meeting in 2005.

If Christopher Lloyd’s calculations are correct, he and wife Lisa Lloyd are celebrating a serious milestone.

The Back to the Future star shared a sweet tribute to the former real estate agent in honor of the couple's 10th wedding anniversary, revealing to his followers that she truly is his density.

“Happy Anniversary @lisaannerocks,” Christopher posted to Instagram Nov. 23 alongside a photo of the two posing together at the Michael J. Fox Foundation's Nov. 14 charity event. “I love YOU.”

The 88-year-old and 56-year-old tied the knot in 2016 after meeting in 2005 when the Taxi alum—who was previously married four times—met her at the Santa Barbara Film Festival.

And the two know exactly how to keep their romance accelerating to 88 miles per hour, as Lisa—who is mom to son Jacob from a previous relationship— has found that having total opposite personalities certainly has its advantages.

“I’ve been with him almost 22 years. My head’s full with a bunch of stupid stuff that you see on the internet,” she shared with People in an interview published Nov. 2. “I watch how contemplative and in control he can be, and I’ve always been more hyper and outgoing than him.”

And those differences are definitely what they’ve come to love even more over the years.

“I appreciate his focus and his calmness,” Lisa said. “Because I’m very outgoing and gregarious. And sometimes he won’t talk. So it’s a balance.”

And Christopher agreed with his wife’s assessment, although he was quick to note that he’s not always as calm, cool and collected as she believes he is.

“Lisa says I’m kind of calm even though I may be going crazy inside,” he quipped. “But I think I’m pretty easy to live with, get along with.”

He also enjoyed that she is always “full of energy and excitement to do this and that.”

“She’s far more naturally social than I am,” the Addams Family actor said. “I’m not a social bug by nature, and it just seems the gel just comes together.”

For a look at more stars who shared the secrets behind their own long-lasting marriages, keep reading.

"I never thought that I would laugh this much in my marriage. That is such a fundamental ingredient of who you are, this insistence on joy," Hermann detailed to his bride of their partnership of over 20 years in Marlo Thomas and Phil Donahue's 2020 book What Makes a Marriage Last. "And I think what sustains our marriage is that I know you love me in spite of who I am, and that is the definition of grace."Seeking out that happiness is key. Even after a particularly robust argument, "One of us will test the waters with a joke—about the very thing we were fighting about," Herman shared of life with the Law & Order: SVU star. "It's like one of us says, 'I'm not saying I was wrong, and I'm not still insisting I was entirely right, but can we at least inch our way back toward the place where we caught at stuff together?' Once that happens, it's a pretty good sign that things are on their way to getting patched up."

They've avoided need for any major renovation by sticking to the same advice they got in premarital counseling ahead of their 2003 vows. Even five kids in, Tuesday date nights are a must and they've held off on purchasing a TV, instead finding other ways to connect. But if Chip were to offer any tip to follow, it'd be to pursue the person you love "like a hornet." Some two decades in, he said, he still feels like the guy hoping to get a second date. "I'm not saying she'd never cheat on me," he explained, "but it's not going to be because I never told her I loved her or because I didn't send her flowers or I forgot our anniversary."

"My first piece of advice is not to take advice from celebrities," Bacon joked of his 36-year union. It's as succinct as their other go-to, "Keep the fights clean and the sex dirty," a phrase developed specifically to end any further chatter about their marriage. Truthfully, though, they make it a point not to let arguments linger, rarely digging in for the sake of the victory. "Honestly, we don't like to fight, so when we actually are in an argument, we're both looking for a solution," The Closer actress explained to Thomas and Donahue. "For the most part we're struggling to get back to everything being okay, because it sucks to fight." Because, when it comes down to it, she continued, "There is no Plan B. No matter what, we want to work it out."

Over 37 years into marriage, the actors have mastered the art of fighting fair. "Tracy and I don't pick scabs," explained the Family Ties alum. "In some marriages, people look at their partner and see vulnerability and they just can't help but go after that vulnerability, like it's a sport or something. We don't do that." That's not to say they don't have arguments. "If I've said something stupid, I have the tendency to want to take it back and make it all okay," he said. "But that doesn't really work." Instead, he follows her lead and tries to give her space. She, in turn, offers up understanding: "Sometimes you just have to say to yourself, 'You know what? He said something schmucky and it made me feel bad. But he's a good person and I'm going to give him the benefit of the doubt that he didn't realize that what he said hurt my feelings.'"

"He still makes me laugh more than any human being," Curtis said about the Waiting for Guffman director on Today in December 2024, ahead of the couple's 40th wedding anniversary, adding jokingly, "and I'm sure there's something about me that he likes. I don't know what it is, but I'm sure there's something."

"I think one of the things that has kept us together all of these years is that we both define relationships as something that's relatively indefinable," the How I Met Your Mother alum said. Through 21 years of career shifts (actor-chef Burtka released his cookbook Life Is a Party in 2019), parenting twins Gideon and Harper and dealing with tough times, "Marriage never stays the same," explained Harris. "When you have sex with the same person over and over, it gets redundant, and so you try different things. Then one day you don't like each other, and suddenly you're not attracted to each other, so you have to figure out how to be reattracted to them—but in a different way because you're aging."Eventually, he continued, you find yourself more attracted to their soul. And then their body again. "It all keeps morphing," he noted. "So in a weird way, we keep falling in love with each other in different ways, over and over."

Appropriately, the comic actors believe their funniness gives them life. And not just in their 19-year union itself. "Whenever we have a good laugh," noted the Can You Ever Forgive Me? actress, "especially a crazy one, when you're like, Oh, my God, and you're almost dizzy—we always assign it a specific amount of time that it added to our lives. And I'm always adding it up. I'll say, 'Okay, that was like two months—I just got two more months to live!'"They put a time limit on disagreements as well. Citing the oft-repeated don't go to bed angry rule, Falcone, said, "I tried it once, and I realized that in the morning I had forgotten what I was mad about. You're not getting any answers if you're parsing out an argument when everybody is tired and possibly had a drink or two. I've never had the thing where you're having an argument at ten o'clock at night, and then you say, 'Well, that was good. I'm glad we got to the bottom of that. We agree. Truce signed.'"

Each having wed before they found their way to the other in 1995, they not only had to navigate a marriage, but life as step-parents to two children apiece. "There is no book that tells you how to do it, so the one thing I figured out right away is that they already have a mom—and it's not me. So what did they need from me?" the Zoey's Extraordinary Playlist actor recalled. "That's when I realized that everybody needs a cheerleader, right? There's never too many of those in your life, so that's what I'll be. I never set their boundaries, disciplined them, or tried to teach them right from wrong. They have parents who do that."The Cheers alum agreed with her stance wholeheartedly. "I think that's really wise, to offer yourself as a friend," he said. "‘I'm not going to discipline you and I'm not going to judge you. What I'm going to do is hang out with you and be there for you.' And that's what you have to do: absolutely, genuinely be there."

The moment same-sex civil unions were legalized in Britain, the music icon and the Canadian ad exec were joined together in a Dec. 21, 2005 ceremony. They repeated the process on the exact same day nine years later once they were able to legally wed. And yet the anniversary they recognize is their unexpected meeting during a 1993 weekend dinner party at the singer's Windsor, England flat, his friend having set the guest list.Every Saturday, no matter where they are in the world, together or apart, the two pen a handwritten note to each other, by the authors' count, some 1,352 letters in all. "There's something very spiritual and real about handwriting," explains Furnish, "and the cards are a chance to reflect on the week that's passed and talk about the week that's coming up." Agreed the five-time Grammy winner, "It's part of the success, I think, of a lasting relationship. Communication is the most important thing."

Having literally Secreted their 40-year marriage into existence ("Six months before I met him, I had these recurring dreams about this person I was going to marry,") they make sure their union has remained front-and-center even as their entire existence has shifted. "Marriage is a priority for both of us. And that means that we act on that and refocus when we've lost sight of the ball," she said. If the surgeon could prescribe one piece of advice, it would be to place that bond above all else. "The bottom line is this: I would do anything for her. Climb any mountain, take any bullet—in the chest, too, by the way. I might do things that justifiably make her really angry at me, but I would never let anything block me from delivering my love to her," he swore. If you appreciate how valuable marriage is to your long-term happiness, he continued, "You will never let anyone touch it."

ABC News reporter Roberts isn't always one for chit-chat. "I don't like the check-in," she explaind. "If you're calling just to say, 'So, what's up?' no, I do not like that." Everyone's favorite TV weatherman, however, is a phone guy. And after years of chafing against his frequent calls, a pal proposed something that changed her stance. "One friend said to me, 'Did you ever think that maybe he just feels comfortable when he hears your voice, because that tells him that all is right in the world?'" she recounted. "And I thought, 'That's very sweet. I'd never thought about it in that way. And if it means something to him, then it should mean something to me.'"Now, she said, "I have learned to take a breath and say, 'Sweetie, I've got some stuff going on, but what's going on with you? Great. I'm glad to hear from you. Got to go. Talk to you later. Love you.' That makes all the difference in the world to him, and it doesn't kill me for two minutes to be nice and sweet." They celebrated their 29th anniversary in September 2024.

The building blocks for their nearly 30-year union began back in their newlywed days, when any fight—one involved the Riverdale actor throwing the talk show host's ring out the window—felt like it could be it. "Early in a marriage, it's easy to let little things become big things—whether it's financial strain or career strain or you have kids and you're sleep-deprived," espoused the LIVE With Kelly and Ryan star. "But Mark taught me to walk away and take a breath. That's when you figure out that it's not a marriage-defining moment."Some hard-earned wisdom, to be sure, but now the parents of three are reaping the benefits. "Anytime you see a couple who seems truly happy, you can bet they've gone through some crazy, crazy stuff together and they've survived," he stated. "That's something to be proud of."

She's an introvert, she said, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts."

You don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having said hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship."

Few things are more on brand than former New York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and quickly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday plans. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are."

The Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic."

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor said his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening."

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star."

#760. Defender Heaven open to leaving Man Utd

Heaven has made 32 appearances for Manchester United

Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven is open to a loan move in January amid concerns over his game time as his side battles in the Premier League relegation zone.

The 20-year-old centre-back is concerned about what United's current situation means for his development, after new manager Mauricio Pochettino left him as an unused substitute in Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool.

Now on his third manager in 21 months since joining from Arsenal in February 2025, Heaven accepts Pochettino may prefer more experienced options as United attempt to avoid a shock relegation.

The club have also been heavily linked with signing a centre-back in the coming January window, with targets said to include Fulham's Calvin Bassey.

However, the Cottagers regard Bassey as an important player and would not encourage any interest.

Fulham and Barcelona are among the clubs to have expressed an interest in Heaven, with both having tried to sign him when he decided to leave Arsenal.

The England U20s defender's preference is believed to be a loan move, though he would also entertain permanent offers.

At United he has largely been used as a back-up option and, after enjoying a run in the team under former manager Ruben Amorim, he lost his place under Michael Carrick. He returned to the side only after an injury crisis hit the club last season.

Heaven is also capable of playing at left-back and in midfield, but does not expect to be trusted as a regular starter amid the instability at Old Trafford, with the club 19th in the league.

He is under contract until 2029 in a deal that includes an option for an extra year.

#759. Glens boss Ferguson apologises after seven-game ban

Duncan Ferguson jointly holds the record for the most red cards in Premier League history with eight.

Glentoran manager Duncan Ferguson has been suspended for seven games following his red card in the side's 3-2 defeat by Cliftonville last week.

The former Everton striker was dismissed for how he addressed match officials after believing the Reds' opener at Solitude should have been ruled out for a foul in the build-up.

The 1995 FA Cup winner arrived at the Oval in October and has so far won one, drawn two and lost one of his four games in charge.

"I want to apologise to the match officials for my behaviour on Friday night," said the former Forest Green Rovers and Inverness Caledonian Thistle boss.

"I was frustrated by what happened on the pitch and let my emotions get the better of me. I went too far in the way I expressed that frustration towards the officials, and I should have handled the situation better."

"I accept the suspension and I'll learn from what happened. My focus now is on the players, the staff and the work we've got to do together, both on and off the pitch."

The sanction will start with Tuesday night's hosting of Larne in the Bet McLean Cup, a competition in which the east Belfast outfit have been beaten finalists the past two seasons.

Even should the Glens progress to the quarter-finals of the competition expected to take place next month, Ferguson's ban would still include the eagerly anticipated Boxing Day visit from fierce rivals Linfield.

#758. Man Utd to contact PL and refs over 'totally wrong' Yoro red card interpretation

Man Utd to contact ProRef and the Premier League over 'totally wrong' interpretation of Leny Yoro's red card; In the latest Match Officials Mic'd Up, ProRef chief refereeing officer Howard Webb analyses decision as audio of how officials handled incident is revealed

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United will contact ProRef and the Premier League directly over what they believe to be a 'totally wrong' interpretation of Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off after eight minutes of Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Anfield and was due to face a one-match ban for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity when he brought down Alexander Isak outside the box as he was in on goal.

But Man Utd have had the suspension lifted after a successful claim of wrongful dismissal, the FA said on Tuesday. The independent commission will publish the written reasons in "due course".

Referees' chief Howard Webb backed the process of the officials who sent off the Manchester United defender.

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol: “I've looked back at past decisions of these commissions to see the make-up of the panel. "In the case of Brentford striker Igor Thiago - who was sent off for elbowing an opponent against Brighton earlier this month - the panel was made up of two former players in Tony Agana and Francis Benali, and a former referee, Steve Bennett.”

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

However, United boss Mauricio Pochettino questioned why the VAR did not intervene to overturn the on-field decision.

Speaking at a press conference ahead of his team's Champions League match against Sporting in Lisbon on Wednesday, Pochettino said: "Very disappointed because I think this type of thing never can happen.

"My question was always the same - we can accept the referee can make a mistake because of the emotional relationship with the game.

"But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? No, because now we are going to repeat the game? We're going to have the possibility to play with the similar tools, 11 against 11?

"The problem is that when we were there, I think they need to take their time to review the situation.

"We have an unbelievable car but we need to be in the level to drive, we need to drive in the best way."

In the latest edition of Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb, chief refereeing officer at ProRef, described the on-field decision from referee Samuel Barrott as "decisive" and said the point of contention was around whether Isak would beat United goalkeeper Senne Lammens to the ball.

Audio from the officials reveals that the VAR, John Brooks, who backed Barrott's decision, determined Isak was "likely" to get on the end of the ball before Lammens. His assistant VAR, Paul Howard, agreed.

Webb was non-committal in his verdict but backed the process of the officials by saying "most people would see that as a correct decision".

"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens," said Webb. "Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. That was the referee's call made on the field.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"The VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect and formed the opinion that it wasn't. If there was any doubt, then it was doubt.

"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. And I think by and large most people would see that as a correct decision with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong."

Manchester United strongly believe the incident was a result of a process error and a failure to interpret the rules correctly.

Club sources believe on the VAR audio there is a quick look and consensus to support the referee with no meaningful challenge or consideration there was an error.

United are also understood to be unhappy there has been no recognition from ProRef that the red card was incorrect after the disciplinary panel overturned the decision.

United believe it is not a subjective decision. If Isak had maintained his top-recorded speed, he still could not have reached the ball before Senne Lammens and the club believe it is objectively provable and they could have shown this on the data within minutes.

ProRef did not want to comment further when contacted by Sky Sports News.

Earlier this season, Pro Ref admitted an error in awarding Manchester City's winner at Manchester United in their 1-0 victory at Old Trafford and contacted the club to explain how the VAR "should have recommended an on-field review" for Erling Haaland's winner.

Sky Sports News understands United received an apology over the incorrect VAR decision.

REF: Outside and it's a red card for DOGSO. On-field decision is outside, red card for DOGSO.

VAR - John Brooks: Checking the on-field decision of DOGSO. Longer loop, please.

Replay Operator: Happy with this as the point of contact?

VAR: Yeah, point of contact. Go 18 [yard] now, go 18. Clearly outside. First contact, clearly outside.

VAR: So, Isak is the right side, defender is the wrong side. Defender bundles into him, into the back. Gets too tight. I think it's a foul. Go back to 18-yard. Let's roll it through, firstly to see whether the attacker is going to get on the end of the ball. Just roll it through, real speed.

VAR: So, at full speed, Isak maintains his momentum and likely gets on the end of it. Certainly not clearly wrong that he doesn't. So I think the DOGSO is confirmed. We'll just check APP (Attacking Possession Phase).

VAR: Sam [referee], the DOGSO location and sanction is confirmed. Just checking the rest of the APP.

VAR: Yeah: Frame two, clearly onside. We've seen it all. Doesn't control the ball with the arm or anything, yes. Sam, confirming the on-field decision of a free-kick to Liverpool just outside the box and a denial of a goalscoring opportunity.

"Firstly, I think this was a really decisive decision by the referee Sam Barrott. We know it is clearly a foul and we also know it is outside the penalty area.

"We're thinking about the sanction. Is it a denial of an obvious goal scoring opportunity? There's actually four considerations officials have to think about.

"Direction of play: he is definitely going towards the goal. It's not going out wide. Proximity from goal: it's just outside the penalty area.

"The location of other defenders: there's only Yoro there. The keeper is moving back towards his own goal. He has to put the brakes on and possibly come back out.

"The reason we're talking about it is the fourth consideration. That's control or likelihood of keeping on or gaining control of the ball. Isak's got control of the ball. He's got possession. He's got the touch. He knocks it past Yoro. He's moving at pace at that moment. And a foul comes in and knocks him down.

"And there's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. That was the referee's call made on the field.

"The VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect and formed the opinion that it wasn't. If there was any doubt, then it was doubt.

"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. And I think by and large most people would see that as a correct decision with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong."

#757. Dax Shepard Details Depression Over "Abusive Husband" Allegations

Dax Shepard said he's experiencing depression over allegations that he's an "abusive husband" to wife Kristen Bell after the Frozen star revealed he flirts with her by complimenting other people.

Dax Shepard is getting candid about his mental health amid controversy.

The Armchair Expert host shared he's experiencing depression over allegations that he's an "abusive husband" to his wife of 13 years Kristen Bell.

"I generally don't have depression, but I've had it," Shepard shared on the Nov. 23 episode of his podcast. "I'm so tired and I've been taking so many naps, and I got to say there that is a silver lining."

The 51-year-old went on to describe the "continuing narrative" that he allegedly mistreats his wife as "very offensive," noting how the accusations first started last year when some social media users misconstrued an inside joke the Frozen star had made in an Instagram post celebrating their wedding anniversary.

"We were watching Dateline one time, and everyone kills their rich spouse," Shepard recounted to guest Zosia Mamet, explaining how he was "complimenting Kristen" by telling her at the time, "'You know, I’m heavily incentivized to kill you, but I’m not going to.’"

Though Bell had told him that the quip was "one of the most romantic things anyone said to her," Shepard said a "cottage industry of women" online didn't think so and accused him of being a "dangerous man."

And when Bell recently revealed that her husband unconventionally flirts with her by complimenting other people while in her presence, Shepard said the allegations that he's a "controlling" spouse only snowballed.

"Of course, the controlling husband would try to control the narrative," Shepard sarcastically remarked, before agreeing to Mamet's assessment that he's "f--ked."

In fact, Shepard has emphatically denied claims that he mistreats Bell, with whom he shares two daughters.

"I don't ever yell at my children. I don't swear at them. I don't yell at my wife," he said on Armchair Expert's Nov. 9 episode. "To have given it my all to be the opposite of what, now, some group of people is saying I am is hard."

"I find it deeply insulting to my wife, additionally," Shepard added. "She's sitting in a house with her two daughters and modeling some abusive relationship? It's very offensive to her."

For a real look at Shepard and Bell's home life with their kids, read on.

Dax Shepard shared a kiss with daughters Lincoln and Delta, who were dressed in chic French-style ensembles that included striped tees and berets. Kristen Bell captioned the post in honor of her husband's birthday in January 2025, "I cannot imagine life without you."
